We've already seen some great holiday adverts as the festive season begins, from the handcrafted stop-motion Levi's Christmas advert, to Prada's cartoon wonderland directed by former Disney animator John Pomeroy. Alas, the historic master of the genre has come up lacking.

In the UK, the arrival of the John Lewis Christmas advert was long seen as the unofficial start of the season. The department store chain features twice in our pick of the best Christmas adverts of all time. But its 2026 offering has sparked a fierce backlash over what people see as confused messaging, with some people even calling for a boycott of the store.

A post shared by John Lewis & Partners (@johnlewis)

Titled Gloria and Pickles, the 2026 John Lewis Christmas advert is an opulent affair. Set to a Sam Fender cover of The Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want, it sees National treasure Kristin Scott Thomas star as a wealthy grandma who can't find anything to entertain her spoiled grandchildren and stop them from messing up her huge, gloomy mansion.

The kids are, naturally, unimpressed by an ancient Fisher-Price Little Snoopy Toy. She's about to give them some cash when the wooden dog turns into canine Chat-GPT with the voice of Paul Whitehouse and admonishes her for the lack of imagination. "Do you want them to like you?" the toy asks her at one point.

Off they go shopping, passing through several sub-standard stores until arriving at John Lewis. There, Kristin spends a fortune on decorations to turn one of her many spare rooms into a festive party space, which convinces the kids to finally show her some affection.

The message is supposed to be that a personal gift is more in keeping with the spirit of Christmas than cold, hard cash. But what comes across is that, either way, spending money is the only way to get you grandkids to like you. Good luck if you can't afford to shop at John Lewis.

According to the creative effectiveness company System 1, the ad achieved 5.6 stars on its rating system, making it John Lewis's strongest-performing festive campaign since Excitable Edgar in 2019. Its testing found that 61% of viewers felt happy watching the advert, nearly twice the UK TV advertising average.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

That's not the impression you get from the comments on social media. Writing on X Piers Morgan (what's the opposite of a national treasure?) described it as "possibly the worst advert I’ve ever seen for anything".

There's some hyperbole there. It least it's not Coca-Cola's AI slop. But he has a point, and a lot of people agree. The family is unlikeable, the children entitled and overindulged, and the materialistic tone feels out of touch amid the cost of living crisis, reminding younger viewers how skint they are (everything from the dog to Kristin's outfits is shoppable). Even the colour grading is depressing.

John Lewis switched from Adam&Eve to Saatchi & Saatchi as its creative agency back in 2023. Unlike the whimsical ads of the past that became such an annual event, this piece feels cold and clinical. It's more obviously geared towards conversion, attempting to shape behaviour by guilt tripping grandparents.

#9028. Solid cork forms walls of pavilion dedicated to silence at Casa No Tempo in Alentejo

Photography by Mercês Tomaz Gomes

Antwerp-based studio Corkinho has unveiled its latest “still room”, a pavilion with walls of solid cork, which is installed in the grounds of a vacation villa designed by Manuel Aires Mateus.

The still room is a space dedicated to silent and introspective activities, such as reading, yoga, tea ceremonies or meditation.

Corkinho installed it in the grounds of Casa No Tempo, a former farmhouse in southern Portugal, which architect Aires Mateus converted into a holiday home in 2014 for hospitality entrepreneur João Rodrigues.

Lead designer Cédric Etienne devised the building’s innovative structure, which is fully demountable, with the help of architect and master carpenter Gonçalo Madeira Marrote of Madeiguincho.

The floor slab is a timber deck, built over a foundation of removable concrete blocks.

Above this, solid blocks of cork are stacked up like giant bricks to form the building’s walls and secured with metal rods that thread through milled channels.

The pavilion is topped by a timber roof, described by Etienne as “like a hat with four screws”, which helps to weigh down the cork blocks.

“I wanted it to be zero waste and carbon-neutral,” the designer told Dezeen.

“If we need to dismantle it, we can place it somewhere else. There is no glue and no screws,” he said.

“It’s like the Japanese way of building teahouses, with total respect of the local materials and no harm to the land.”

As the name suggests, Corkinho is a studio that specialises in objects and spaces built from cork.

The studio first launched the still room concept in 2020, when it moved its office into the former Noorderpershuis power station in Antwerp and transformed one of the rooms into a silent sanctuary.

Etienne defines a still room as any space where you can pause your mind and be still.

“It’s a place where you disconnect from noise and distractions and invite a deeper sense of presence,” he said.

After consulting with various hotel brands keen to adopt the concept, Etienne pitched the idea to Rodrigues and his company, Silent Living.

The company has five properties, all designed by Aires Mateus and all with a focus on slow living.

“I had been to Casa No Tempo many times, so I knew the place like an inner home,” the designer said.

“It felt so aligned in terms of feeling and senses, so I thought it could be a really beautiful challenge to move the concept forward in this place,” he continued.

The room can be used by guests staying at the villa, but it can also accommodate curated programmes.

Etienne has been hosting four-day silent retreats, allowing groups of designers and hospitality professionals to learn more about the still room concept.

The cork blocks, supplied by locally based company Sofalca, were heat-treated to improve their durability. The material gives the building impressive sensorial and thermal qualities, Etienne said.

“All the technical properties of cork – the acoustics, the scent, the softness – all become architectural conditions,” he stated.

“You really feel like you’re coming into a womb. Even when it’s 40 degrees outside, the temperature inside is around 22 or 23.”

Other pavilions recently featured in Dezeen include a wildlife pavilion informed by rippling water and a jigsaw-like pavilion made of mass-timber scrap.

#9027. Georgia O’Keeffe Painting Found in Closet After 40 Years Heads to Christie’s With $ 3 M. Est.

When Christie’s holds its 20th Century Evening Sale in two weeks, one painting will hit the block with a curious story. The Georgia O’Keeffe painting Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930) only recently resurfaced after nearly 40 years out of the public eye.

Per the New York Post, the painting was found by a Rhode Island woman when she was helping her elderly aunt clear her East Village apartment. According to the 65-year-old woman, who the Post names only by her middle name, Betsy, she found the painting at the back of a closet under a row of fur coats. Related Articles Gloria Steinem's Life in Art What We Miss When We Flatten Georgia O'Keeffe Into a Feminist Icon

“I thought, wow, that’s that’s pretty wild,” she told the Post. “I wondered, ‘Is there any way I can keep this?’ … But once we started exploring what the value of the piece was, I realized that it’s worth more than my house.”

According to the woman, her aunt told her in 2022 off-handedly that there was an O’Keeffe painting in the closet as they prepped the house for home health aides. However, Betsy didn’t actually find the work until a few weeks ago when her aunt was put into hospice at age 98.

The aunt, who has since died, was once a Foreign Services worker. She recieved the painting as a graduation gift from her mother in 1963, when she purchased it from The Downtown Gallery on 51st Street for $3,800. As Betsy tells it, the painting hung in the apartment until the 1980s, when she noticed a guest “eyeing it a bit too closely.”

“I think she was fully aware of its value … she recognized that it was an expression of her financial position,” Betsy said.

The painting has since become a bit of an oddity for Betsy and her family, who says she hung it up “for chuckles.” “The men in the family who’ve seen this have commented, there seems to be a number of ‘vaginas’ in the picture,” she said

The painting carries a $2 million to $3 million estimate, and a portion of the proceeds will be donated to an unnamed educaiton institution. The rest will go towards Betsy and her family “for things like paying off the mortgage.” Fair enough.

In a lot essay, Christie’s described the painting as an “important early work” that is “likely the first iteration in a series of three works depicting Lobo Peak, north of Taos Pueblo.” One of the other such works is in the collection of MoMA, while the other is in an unamed private collection.

#9026. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#9024. Archaeologists Discover Vast Ice Age Cave Art Hiding in Plain Sight

Archaeologists have discovered one of the largest assemblages of Ice Age rock art ever recorded in the Iberian Mediterranean, shedding new light on population sizes and regional artistic expression during the Paleolithic. The 2019 find, made at the tourist attraction Cova de la Font Major in Catalonia, was described in the journal Antiquity this month.

Although more than half of the Paleolithic rock art recorded in Europe is in the Iberian Peninsula, it was long believed to be rare in the north-eastern part of the region. Comprising 280 figurative and nonfigurative rock engravings, the discovery at Cova de la Font Major has upended this assumption, suggesting not only a larger population than previously thought, but one with its own artistic traditions. Related Articles 12,000-Year-Old Clothing Made of Animal Hide Discovered in Ice Age Caves in Oregon British Museum to Loan 'Some of the Rarest Surviving Examples' of Ice Age Art to UK's 2025 City of Culture

As attested to by the numerous engravings and graffiti on its walls, have been visiting the Cova de la Font Major for at least 900 years. Although its main entrance collapsed at some point during the Roman period (2nd–5th centuries CE), an inscription dated 1199 indicates an entry in the second millennium CE, perhaps through a fissure or other access point.

In 1853, the Cova de la Font Major was entered through a private well, but only sporadic visits to it are recorded until 1956, when it was explored and surveyed by members of the Centre Excursionista Pirinenc. In 1957 the town council of Espluga de Francolí cleared the entrance to provide access to visitors, and in 1993 the cave was converted to a museum.

In 2011, researchers confirmed that part of the entrance, destroyed in 1957, had survived, leading to the inclusion of the site in a 2018 research project. The Ice Age engravings were discovered during the project’s excavation campaign the following year, when one of the authors noticed that among the various graffiti on the cave walls some looked Paleolithic.

“For more than six decades, thousands of visitors passed directly in front of the engraved surfaces, and in some cases inscribed names and dates over them, without the Paleolithic origin of the figures being recognized,” writes research co-author Josep Maria Vergès from the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA).

Located in series of small galleries within the cave, the engravings consist of depictions of various animals as well as groupings of abstract marks, including a particularly distinctive composition, comprising hundreds of loop-shaped incisions. Moreover, while uneven conglomerate rock like that at Cova de la Font Major is theoretically unsuitable for cave art, here the artists incorporated its irregularities into their compositions, using junctures of two different kinds of rock as ground lines for figures, for example, or turning a fissure into a water surface, as in one rendering of drinking deer.

“The Mediterranean art of western Europe is now enriched by a new body of rock art,” states Vergès, “which allows us to characterize in greater depth a Mediterranean graphic tradition with an identity of its own.”

Malika Favre and Kumkum Fernando blend music, mythology and '60s flower power.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Forty years ago, Montreux Jazz Festival brought together the great US pop artists Andy Warhol and Keith Haring to create the poster design for the annual event. The result was a vibrant fusion of styles celebrating jazz music and rhythm. Now, the festival has repeated the experiment for just a second time, uniting two acclaimed contemporary artists for a dream collaboration.

The 2027 poster design was created by the French illustrator Malika Favre and the Sri Lankan sculptural artist and designer Kumkum Fernando. The former's distinctive geometric graphic style merges with the latter's colourful retrofuturism in a striking maximalist design that channels diverse influences into the form of a divine being that represents music as a joyful, spiritual journey.

Montreux has a long history of artist-designed posters. Other previous contributors have included David Bowie, Jean Tinguely, Yoann Lemoine (Woodkid), Lakwena, Kévin Germanier and Christian Marclay.

Keith Haring designed for the festival twice. For his second commission, in 1986, he worked with Andy Warhol as a collaborator. The festival invited Malika to adopt a similar approach for her second contribution, ten years after her first design for Montreux.

While her 2017 poster stood out for its minimalism, the new design goes in the opposite direction. A densely packed arrangement of colour and shapes creates a fantastical figure that looks like a cross between a robot, sacred altar and a jukebox. In fact, the design is also being turned into a sculptural vinyl cabinet (see further below).

“I fell in love with the festival on my very first visit in 2017. The poster I created for that edition remains one of my personal favourites to this day. I knew it would be hard to match, so I wanted to take the opposite approach: to create a work bursting with colour, as maximalist as the first one was minimalist. Kumkum was the ideal artist for this,” Favre says of the collaboration.

The design draws on diverse influences, including South Asian traditions, retro-futurism and '60s counterculture. The flowers evoke the lakeside quays of Montreux but also the flower power movement of the hippie era, a nod to the fact that Montreux Jazz Festival was founded during the 1967 Summer of Love. The floral patterns also subtly outline lips, kisses and female faces – symbols of love, pleasure and sexuality that recur throughout Malika's artistic universe.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

“I had this vision of music blooming in Montreux, this feeling of the entire town coming alive during the festival,” Favre adds. “I wanted to convey that joy. The world is going through strange times, and a festival like Montreux is an opportunity to celebrate. For me, flowers also symbolise eroticism, an explosion of the senses and the pleasures found in music. I always like to tuck in something a little cheeky, and I thought I could bring that touch of a feminine sensuality. When I sent the first flowers to Kumkum he said, ‘Oh yes, that’s sexy!’”

From the outset, the idea was also to bring the poster’s divine entity into the world as a three-dimensional object, following Kumkum’s practice of creating futuristic, geometric sculptures. The result is a made-for-order vinyl cabinet with a dedicated turntable compartment and pull-out drawers for record storage.

“The spark came when we noticed the resemblance between the shape of certain religious altars and that of a jukebox, both sharing the same sense of symmetry,” Fernando says. “We imagined a kind of gateway into a sacred realm of music, a timeless entity, part retro-futuristic robot, part mythological being, that embodies music as a joyful, universal experience.”

The 61st Montreux Jazz Festival will take place on the Lake Geneva shoreline from 2 July to 17 July 2027.

#9022. Paris Court Orders Sotheby’s to Return Nazi-Looted Pissarro Painting to Jewish Heirs

A Paris court has ordered the restitution of a painting by Camille Pissarro, allegedly seized by the Nazis during World War II, to the descendants of Jewish banker and art collector Salomon Flavian, reports Le Figaro. A group of his heirs sued Sotheby’s in Paris in September, saying they were improperly left out of an agreement struck with other members of their family

The case concerns the French Impressionist’s 1902 canvas Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, Dieppe, après-midi ensoleillée (Fishing dock and Duquesne basin, Dieppe, sunny afternoon), showing the port city in western France. Related Articles A Rare Albrecht Altdorfer Painting Heads to Sotheby's for $6.67 M. A Seagram Heir, a Bankrupt Hedge Funder, and More: Consignors for the November Marquee Sales Revealed

Sotheby’s London sold the painting in 2024 for £1.2 million ($1.5 million at the time). The auctioneer indicated that the work was being offered “pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian,” whose collection the Nazis seized in Paris in 1941. The house’s lawyers maintained in court that the heirs’ consent was gained through Mondex Corporation, which specializes in the recovery of art and other assets looted during World War II, reported the Art Newspaper. But seven plaintiffs maintained in court in September that only two relatives, Gilles and Nicholas Flavian, had signed the agreement and that the rest had not been consulted, per the newspaper.

In its Thursday decision, the court nullified all sales since the initial seizure of the painting, and ordered the return of the work. It concluded that the Flavian family established that Salomon had owned the painting, that it had been confiscated by the Germans, and that he had taken steps to recover his assets after the war. The court ordered Sotheby’s to inform the family of the identity of the buyer in the 2024 sale, or be fined €1,000 ($1,123) per day thereafter, reports Le Figaro, noting that the judgment applies immediately, even in the event of an appeal.

In an email to ARTnews, Mondex Corporation consultant James Palmer said that an appeal will be filed “forthwith.” Palmer argued that the archives of dealer Paul Rosenberg and the 1939 Pissarro catalogue raisonné “both clearly identify [British artist and collector] Edward Le Bas as the owner of the painting from 1939 to the early 1950s.” This means the painting could not have been seized from Flavian during the 1940s, he says.

“Of great importance is the fact that France currently lacks a formal restitution framework, which disadvantages both the state and claimants,” he added, contrasting France with existing adjudication bodies in the UK, Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and the Netherlands, which, he said, “operate on a crucial general principle: that the benefit of the doubt is presumed in the claimant’s favor unless there is evidence to the contrary.”

Regarding Le Bas’s ownership, he continued, “These crucial facts were not commented upon by the court in its decision and can therefore be presumed to have been given no significant consideration, which is a flaw in the judicial assessment of the case. We are confident that when the vast amount of complex provenance research evidence is properly understood and considered that the court of appeal will reach a different conclusion.”

#9021. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

#9020. Many London architecture firms not paying London Living Wage

The majority of the London-based studios in The Pay 100‘s fifth annual salary survey are not paying Part I architectural assistants the London Living Wage, as required by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA).

An engineering firm has topped the leaderboard for the average salaries for UK architects, according to a survey conducted by the anonymous group The Pay 100.

Engineering firm tops architect salary leaderboard

Published over the weekend, the survey provides rough figures only based on the mean figures submitted by respondents. This year’s data collected the annual salary of 127 firms in the UK and the mean number of hours of unpaid overtime per week.

Topping the leaderboard with the highest average annual salary for architects with less than five years’ experience is BakerHicks, an engineering and design firm, which paid £72,000, according to the survey.

Second on the list is London studio Hawkins\Brown at £63,700, and joint third at £56,300 are London practices Samuel Chisholm Studio and Thomas Alexander Design.

The survey also presented figures for Part I and Part II architectural assistants. Transport for London had the highest wage for Part II roles at £44,000, followed by Foster + Partners at £42,000.

Majority of London firms not paying London Living Wage

The results for Part I roles included salaries from 30 studios, 21 of which were based in Greater London.

Only the top four studios on the leaderboard – Haworth Tompkins, Allford Hall Monaghan Morris, Studio McW and Studio PDP – paid more than the London Living Wage of £32,136, which RIBA declared a requirement for relevant offices.

Twelve of the 30 studios were paying Part I roles less than the £29,328 UK Living Wage.

Low wages “a threat to the future of the profession”

Alongside its survey data, The Pay 100 wrote an open letter to RIBA, asking it to take action on the financial wellbeing of those working in the architecture industry and to ensure the long-term future of the profession.

“Our aim has always been to create tangible financial incentives for employers to improve pay, empower employees to make informed career decisions, and encourage a healthier, more sustainable profession,” said The Pay 100 in the letter.

“We recognise that architecture practices operate within a highly competitive market, often under significant financial pressure themselves,” it continued. “Nevertheless, the commercial challenges facing practices should not prevent the profession from addressing the deteriorating conditions experienced by many employees.”

“Poor financial conditions for staff are not merely an employment issue; they are a threat to the long-term health, resilience and future of the profession.”

It went on to set out two courses of action it called for RIBA to take: establishing “meaningful minimum salaries” for RIBA chartered practices, and taking full ownership of The Pay 100 and its annual salary survey.

The Pay 100 said a framework of minimum salary levels should be established across different architecture roles, increasing year-on-year in line with inflation.

“A profession cannot sustainably advocate for the value of its services while leaving the financial conditions of its workforce to market pressures alone,” it said. “The RIBA should take a leading role in addressing this imbalance.”

After five years of aiming to improve pay transparency with its annual surveys, The Pay 100 wants RIBA to take ownership of the survey and commit resources to it, developing it into an industry-wide initiative.

“We believe that improving pay transparency across UK architecture should be a core responsibility of the profession’s leading membership body,” said The Pay 100.

“Under the RIBA’s stewardship, the survey could benefit from significantly greater reach, sustained institutional support and broader participation across the profession,” it continued.

“This would provide a foundation for more comprehensive salary data, stronger engagement between employers and employees, and meaningful progress towards better financial conditions throughout the industry.”

The Pay 100 ended its letter by asking for a public response from RIBA by 1 December

A Brighton studio of Northerners, a 25-hour RPG and a free game engine. It’s set in 2002, so nobody has a smartphone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Plenty of Pokémon imitators have come along over the years, with the most brazen in recent years being Palworld. But look at 2023's Cassette Beasts, and you see how a creature-collecting game can offer a unique twist without following the same mascot-based formula. For one, it wasn't really about catching creatures but recording and then transforming into them yourself. Speaking to Bytten Studio's co-founder, art and game director Jay Bayliss, it had been important very early on to consider how Cassette Beasts would distinguish itself.

"We had the idea of fusion as a central mechanic, which Pokemon can't tap into because Pikachu is a mascot that you can't dilute by merging it with a thousand other beasts to get new beasts," he explains. "We also thought about focusing on the human characters, so maybe the beasts could be a reflection of the human characters, which led to the idea of transforming into them."

It also helped that Cassette Beasts aimed itself at a slightly older audience compared to every Pokemon game always having you start out as yet another schoolkid, though its British humour and sensibilities also stood out, which is something the Brighton-based studio is leaning even more directly on with its upcoming sequel.

Cassette Beasts 2002 is set in London (as well as its alternate world of Nodnol), but it aims not to give the tourist version of the capital, but a quieter Zone 6 suburb version of it, with the town of Elmwich.

"We don't lean into a certain Paddington-esque twee Britishism about it," Bayliss explains. "Crucially, we're Northerners living down South in Brighton; we don't really play with that twee Britishness. We enjoy portraying quite a mundane, crappy version of suburban English life. We're so bored of the Harry Potter-esque upper middle-class boarding school fantasy take on it. I think this version's more fun."

As the title's palindrome suggests, Cassette Beasts 2002 is also set in 2002. That appeals to me personally, much like one of my favourite indie games released earlier this year, Perfect Tides: Station to Station, because it taps into my formative teen years. "The early 2000s also mark this crossing point between the analogue and digital age," Bayliss explains. "The internet exists, but you don't have smartphones. People do have mobile phones in the game, but we haven't got the Panopticon of social media. For artists younger than me, they reflect on this ethereal time they just missed out on, just before we had the baggage of the modern world overwhelming you."

It was also important to reflect the era's aesthetic and fashion. "Skewing male, game developers often don't appreciate fashion, but if you go on TikTok and social media, people are very interested in noughties fashion," Bayliss explains. "There's a lot of interest in exploring that time that we don't discount, and that's reflected in the fashion sensibilities of the characters and the character designs themselves as well."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Perhaps a major visual shift with this sequel is a more 3D one. Well, it's a case of perspective, literally. The original Cassette Beasts, while presented in the traditional top-down perspective of classic Pokemon and other 8- and 16-bit RPGs, was actually made in a 3D engine, albeit with environments given pixelated textures to match its 2D character sprites. In Cassette Beasts 2002, the camera drops down so things are presented as a third-person 3D game, except its characters are still pixel-art sprites presented with a billboarding technique.

"We were like, what if we can design this game with higher resolution sprites, with eight directions so when you pan the camera around, it feels less awkward?" Bayliss explains. "From a technical point of view, you have to rethink how you're designing worlds, but suddenly the perspective and scale you have in these worlds is very different. If you took the first game and dropped the camera down, it would probably feel very small, so it changes how we sculpt and design the world."

Cassette Beasts 2002 is also developed with the open-source Godot engine, which more indies are turning to. Although Bayliss recalls the challenges of porting the game's predecessor, which was developed with Godot 3, the latest iteration, Godot 4, that the studio is using has greatly improved features, including porting and performance, that make it a more viable alternative to Unity.

"If you sign up to Unity, you're kind of on the hook for any changes that Unity makes, whereas with an open-source engine, if you don't like changes, you can change the engine," Bayliss explains. "I think the flexibility of Godot is what allows a team of two full-time developers to make a big 25-hour RPG. It's just a very uncomplicated engine - you make stuff, you put it in, it's in the game. If there's anything that you need to fix, you don't have to submit a bug report to the back-end team and hope they fix it in the next two years; you just go in and fix it yourself."

Cassette Beasts 2002 is releasing in March 2027 for PC, Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, and Nintendo Switch 2. You can wishlist it now on Steam.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

#9018. Trump Convenes Final Review for Triumphal Arch, Seeks Immediate Start on Construction

President Donald Trump’s planned 250-foot-tall triumphal arch could win approval as soon as Thursday, after he bulldozed a mountain of opposition to secure a final review by a federal commission. Approval would clear the way for construction to begin immediately, though a federal judge could still block the project, as some on Capitol Hill hope.

Washington, D.C., media reported that the Trump-allied National Capital Planning Commission began reviewing plans for the arch on Thursday afternoon, just two days after Republicans lost control of the Senate and the House of Representatives in seismic midterm elections. The commission is expected to approve the plans following lengthy public testimony. Meanwhile, the project’s opponents have called on the federal courts to halt it before construction can begin. Related Articles Arlington County Board Files Lawsuit to Stop Construction of Trump's Triumphal Arch After Resignation of Advisory Council, American Institute of Architects Weigh in on Trump's Arch

“The Court should not allow this lawless project to evade scrutiny,” Brian Schwalb and Jay Jones, the attorneys general of D.C. and Virginia, respectively, wrote in a joint court filing on Wednesday, as reported by the Washington Post.

The structure would rise at Memorial Circle, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, to a height that critics say would cast shadows over the surrounding memorial landscape at various times of day. In recent weeks, the president has reimagined the project as a “military complex,” complete with a sniper’s nest.

Trump first announced plans for the triumphal arch more than a year ago, presenting it as a necessary tribute to the nation’s 250th anniversary. A project of this magnitude would traditionally require congressional approval, which the president has not sought. D.C. lawmakers, historic preservationists, and veterans’ groups argue that the project has been illegally advanced and threatens the site’s solemn character.

In a lawsuit filed last month, the Arlington County Board argued that the arch would “directly obstruct[ing] the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that was deliberately created to symbolize the nation’s post-Civil War reunification.”

The Trump administration maintains that the arch is authorized by century-old plans approved by Congress to commemorate the nation’s reunification after the Civil War. Critics, however, have pointed out that the lawmakers’ plans called for a pair of columns, not a triumphal arch of the kind the president has likened to France’s Arc de Triomphe, “but better, more beautiful actually, much more beautiful.”

Mark Paoletta, a White House official who was appointed commission chairman in August, reportedly said on Thursday that the empty space at Memorial Circle “dishonors our veterans and leaves a key monumental gateway to Arlington that Congress authorized uncompleted.” He added that it was a “national disgrace” that such a landmark was not already standing, praising the president’s “historic vision.”

The Arlington County Board’s lawsuit, which names the National Park Service, as a defendant, accuses the administration and its official of failing to consider the arch’s potential risks to regional flight paths and its impact on emergency services.

“Using the Arch to store large stockpiles of ammunition and as a staging point for drones and snipers, so close to commuters and tourists, will dramatically worsen these public-safety harms and the risk of accidents,” the lawsuit warns.

#9017. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

#9016. Brick bathhouse by Kengo Kuma nears completion in Copenhagen

Pyramidal towers frame pools at the Kai Water Culture House by Japanese studio Kengo Kuma & Associates, which is nearing completion in Copenhagen.

Set to open on the city’s harbour in December, the 5,800-square-metre aquatic centre will contain ten indoor and outdoor pools, alongside wellness facilities and cultural spaces.

Kengo Kuma & Associates was commissioned alongside Danish firms Cornelius Vöge, Søren Jensen and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects to realise the new cultural and recreational facility on the city’s artificial island of Christiansholm – known locally as Papirøen, or Paper Island.

Photos revealed ahead of the opening show the facility’s five staggered buildings perched atop a glazed base and fronted by a wooden pier that provides direct access to the sea.

“The Water Culture House is a significant new landmark on Copenhagen’s waterfront,” Kengo Kuma & Associates lead architect Yuki Ikeguchi said. “It is part of the story of the city and the harbour’s transformation from an industrial to a cultural harbour.”

“As the cultural cornerstone of Papirøen, the house is a gathering place with water and community as its focal point, embraced by a public harbour bath,” Ikeguchi added.

Constructed from 300,000 handmade bricks, the tapered volumes are punctuated by triangular and square openings that filter dappled light into the indoor pools.

“The bricks are arranged in a staggered, stepped pattern, giving the building its distinctive texture and sculptural character,” Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects said.

“A total of 403 windows of varying sizes act as viewing apertures, framing the surroundings and creating captivating experiences of natural light as it shifts throughout the day,” it added.

The tallest of the five volumes, dubbed the Culture Tower, houses the centre’s cultural programmes, which include a third-floor events space. Meanwhile, the other four towers each house lofty indoor pools.

Nestled between the five brick volumes on the first floor is an outdoor pool, framed by the building’s sloped facades, and an open-air Onsen – a Japanese-style hot spring – that overlooks the harbour.

The Kai Water Culture House is set to open to the public on 5 December, with its wooden pier slated for completion early next year.

The facility sits among a wider redevelopment of Copenhagen’s Paper Island led by Danish studio COBE. Recent projects on the island include a 20,000-square-metre apartment complex informed by the area’s 300-year-old warehouses.

#9015. Sweden Returns Benin Bronze Trove to Nigeria, Indigenous Remains to Bolivia

The Swedish government is set to return 40 sacred artifacts from the Kingdom of Benin to Nigeria, marking one of the largest repatriations of the so-called Benin Bronzes.

Nigerian media report that the artworks are expected to be received by a delegation from the Benin Palace in Lagos today, a development that Oba Ewuare II, the monarch of Benin, described as years in the making. Since ascending to the throne, Ewuare has advocated fiercely for the return of bronze sculptures, ceremonial objects, and ivory carvings—collectively known as the Benin Bronzes—from museum and private collections worldwide, with considerable success. Related Articles Buddhas and Dinosaur Bones Among Dozens of Smuggled Artifacts Repatriated to China Met Museum Repatriates Five Pieces of Looted Cretan Armor to Greece

“We have been trying, through my grandfather’s efforts, to bring back our artifacts,” Ewuare said in a statement. “My grandfather succeeded, my father succeeded more, and I think now history is obvious to everybody. We are doing our best to triple and triple all those efforts of our forefathers.”

The Kingdom of Benin was looted of roughly 5,000 royal and religious objects in 1897 by British forces on a punitive expedition through what is now Nigeria. Dispersed through illicit channels among museums and private collections worldwide, the artifacts have become emblematic of efforts by formerly colonized countries to reclaim their cultural heritage, as well as the broader—and often contentious—debate over the ethics of ethnographic collections. In recent years, public sympathies have seemingly shifted toward formerly colonized countries, prompting a wave of repatriations. Museums across the United States, as well as institutions in the Netherlands, Germany, and Switzerland, have returned Benin Bronzes and other ethnographic objects to their countries of origin.

The Swedish government also announced today that it will return 77 objects belonging to the Kallawaya people, including human remains, to the Archaeological Museum in La Paz, Bolivia. The remains were taken out of Bolivia illegally and remained in the collection of the World Culture Museum until 2023, when the Swedish government announced their transfer of ownership.

#9013. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

#9012. Tate Britain’s ’90s Show Is All Scene, No Substance

There is a source of tension raging across the art world lately: the conflict between accessibility and anti-intellectualism, as museums face the challenge of making art feel less elitist, less cold, and less boring without dumbing down to the point of meaninglessness. Tate Britain’s latest exhibition, “The 90s: Art and Fashion,” falls hard on the side of meaningless anti-intellectualism.

The exhibition is curated by Edward Enninful, who was most recently editor-in-chief of British Vogue but, more importantly for this exhibition, became the fashion director of the magazine i-D at the age of 18 in 1990 and led it through the turbulent, dynamic decade that is the subject of his show. Tate has never worked with a celebrity curator in this way before, and Enninful’s presence is strangely felt throughout the exhibition. A wedding gift he received from Steve McQueen—a photograph of McQueen’s hands—hangs on a wall. Many, many i-D spreads are in cases throughout the galleries, some including photographs of Enninful. There is a striking focus on Black masculinity, which is the prism through which Enninful experienced the ’90s. Yet his subjectivity is not clearly articulated, leaving one to wonder: Is it his voice we are sensing through the wall texts and object labels, or is it a more neutral “museum” voice? Is Enninful the subject of the exhibition, via his presence in the lives of the artists and models represented here, or is he the curator? Related Articles 50 Artworks by Artists Who Lived and Worked in India Gifted to the Tate Tate Scoops Up Works by Michaela Yearwood-Dan, Luis Fernando Zapata at Frieze London

Being a museum curator is a job that does, actually, require expertise. (I speak with the bias of being one myself). It is a powerful, often invisible role that shapes perceptions of truth and cultural meaning. The trend toward treating it as a celebrity hobby or a passion project is symptomatic of the current wider social phobia of experts and intellectuals. Throughout this exhibition, Enninful contradicts himself: The decade of the ’90s in Britain was about “critiquing commercialism,” but it was also about groundbreaking ad campaigns. It was about “challenging beauty standards,” but also “democratizing beauty.” No point of distinction between fine art and visual culture is identified in Enninful’s show, so fashion, commercial and personal photography, and fine art share space. That could be interesting—it could be a critical choice—but instead it feels like an oversight.

The art and visual culture in this show generally does something. It either embraces or rejects commercialism. It tells a new, sometimes important, story of race, class, or gender in Britain. It highlights what one wall text ambiguously describes as “importance of intimacy in turbulent times.” But is it good? Not especially. Enninful seems to have gone out of his way to choose bad works. Helen Chadwick, a largely good artist, is represented by two works that rank among her weakest. A cast of a hot water bottle that represents a torso by Rachel Whiteread, a really good artist, somehow manages to be the best thing in the show (along with Chris Ofili’s 1998 painting No Woman, No Cry). Small, quotidian, and tactile, it evokes absence and presence at once, the bitter fleetingness of modern life.

But most of the stuff in these galleries? The endless snapshots of parties, wallpaper covered in butts, the many photographs of Kate Moss, videos of fashion shows, enlarged ad campaign stills—very little of it is good. It conveys a certain nostalgia for a heady era, and it makes a strong case for Enninful’s relevance to it. He knew everyone who is anyone, it seems. But that doesn’t make what he chose to show good art, or even art at all. It’s odd, because the ’90s were famously good years for British art: the time of the YBAs and a shifting and condensing sense of British identity, of optimism and progress. The decade fueled the founding of Tate Modern and Frieze London in the early 2000s, and has led to London’s current position as a nexus of international artists and remarkable historic and contemporary art spaces. You would not know that from this exhibition.

Art museums have to fight for relevance in our new attention economy, just like everything else. We are constantly asked to defend them, to make a case for their purpose. With this exhibition, Tate situates the museum alongside the celebrity economy of influence. Supposedly celebrating the last “analog” decade, it instead feels like an act of surrender to the perceived glibness of the digital age. Old-fashioned as it may seem, I don’t think we should equate art with “content.” There is always an appetite for great art, and there is also always an appetite to consider whether, and why, art is great or not. To join the tide of anti-intellectualism that refuses to take this seriously or rise to the challenge of doing so, as Tate has done with this exhibition, is a grave shame.

Apple's first-ever touchscreen MacBook is finally here! Find my hands-on impressions below, and scroll down for rolling coverage as reactions from critics and creators start to pour in across the web.

They said they wouldn't do it. A touchscreen MacBook has been rumoured since the dawn of time (well, the noughties), but, in a quote that's been infinitely dredged up across the internet over the last couple of weeks, Steve Jobs himself decried the concept as "ergonomically terrible". But Jobs also famously asked, "Who wants a stylus?" And the answer among millions of Apple Pencil users seems to be a resounding, "Us!"

And after a few days with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, I'm happy to report that this is very much a device—perhaps even the ultimate device—for creatives. But rather than the ability to touch the screen, it's all about the quality of that 'PROLED' display itself. Turns out there's a reason Apple decided to lead with that, and not touch, in the name of the device.

Simply put, it's the best laptop screen I've ever seen. With up to 2000 nits of peak brightness, 10,000,000:1 contrast, and P3 + Adobe RGB colour, this is a best-in-class display that puts every other OLED laptop screen I've used to shame. It gives creatives a portable reference-quality display, which means it recreates video, colour and contrast as faithfully as possible. Once you've used the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, everything else looks washed-out in comparison, and for that reason alone it's impossible not to recommend for creatives – so long as the small matter of the $2,899 starting price isn't a barrier.

When it comes to touch, as I've written before, in my testing I've found it to be a nice-to-have rather than a need-to-have. Now that we're all touchscreen natives (which wasn't so much the case when Jobs made those comments in 2010), certain navigational actions just feel right, even on a laptop. Scrolling through windows, pinching to zoom in on a photo or map, scrubbing through the timeline in Final Cut Pro; there are plenty of times when touching the screen feels more intuitive than reaching for the trackpad. And Apple's subtle UI tweaks, such as having navigational icons expand when touched, make the whole thing feel more natural.

But equally, there were plenty of times when I preferred to use the trackpad – particularly when a certain level of accuracy was required. And despite Apple claiming to have produced a newly designed hinge with greater stability, it still wobbles. There's just no getting around the fact that a touchscreen on a vertical display is less ergonomic than it is on a flat one.

From a design perspective, the new MacBook Pro isn't a game-changer – unless you really missed the illuminating Apple logo (another noughties mainstay). There are improvements here and there; the Dynamic Island takes up less space than the notch, and slightly smaller bezels result in slightly larger viewing areas. But perhaps the most meaningful design change is the reduction in weight. That OLED panel has allowed for a 14% weight loss – making the 14-inch model, somewhat ironically, lighter than the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air.

But everything pales next to the screen. The PROLED XDR looks incredible. If you're looking for the most impressive visual fidelity available on a laptop, here it is. You can touch it if you like.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is released tomorrow, with preorders available now. Prices start at $2899 for the 14-inch model, and $3399 for the 16-inch model.

Of course, it's a very pricey machine. But reportedly, Apple is trying to find ways to bring down the price in the future by using HMO thin-film transistor technology for OLED panels. It's a piece of tech also being considered by Samsung and LG to make OLED screens cheaper. Here's hoping.

What's that? You're looking for an ASMR unboxing of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display? Whatever floats your boat.

If you're tempted by that awesome new display (or, if you like, the touchscreen), you can go ahead and order the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display at Amazon right now, starting at $2899.

We were lucky enough to attend the launch of the MacBook PROLED with XDR display in Los Angeles last week. There, among other things, we saw... Apple CEO John Ternus signing iPhones? Sure. Okay, then.

Our sister site T3 is also waxing lyrical about the new MacBook Pro, but this time it isn't the touchscreen or the XDR display that's getting the most rapturous response – it's the reduction in weight:

"I brought my personal M3 MacBook Pro to the hands-on to compare it to, and hefting them both side-by-side, the loss of around 300g of weight between generations is really quite significant. On the one hand, you might not notice it explicitly... but everything adds up, and it makes a genuine difference."

It seems that even after a short time, there's something of a critical consensus: come for the touchscreen, stay for the display.

And the YouTubers' reviews are making their way online too. Here's renowned Apple fan/creator iJustine's take. Like many, she's a fan of the glowing Apple logo.

And here's our sister site Tech Radar with, again, a very similar take: "While all the talk is about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display being the first MacBook with a touchscreen, the touchscreen is arguably not its most interesting feature; it works fine, but macOS is still an operating system built for traditional laptop inputs. Instead, it’s the gorgeous tandem OLED screen and industry-leading battery life that should get you excited here."

The Verge's review is up, and it seems they share our opinion: the screen is incredible, the thinner and lighter design is welcome, and touch is... there. "Even if you love the touchscreen, you’ll use it a lot for a day or so and go back to using your laptop almost exactly the way you did before."

Hello and welcome to Creative Bloq's coverage of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. We'll be keeping this page updated with opinions from across the web, but for now, what do we think? In short, touch is nice, but it's that PROLED display that's the killer here. It's the brightest (and darkest) laptop screen we've ever used – and for creatives, having a portable reference-quality display could be a game-changer.

#9010. Here’s How Major Galleries’ UK Operations Performed in 2025

The good news: The United Kingdom is still the world’s second-largest art market by value, according to the latest Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report. The not-so-good news? Since 2009, UK sales have grown just 14 percent, while the United States market has grown 51 percent.

The art market seesaw keeps tilting. This fall, many galleries with UK branches filed their annual reports with Companies House, the UK government agency that keeps records for businesses registered in the country. Some, like David Zwirner, Lisson, and Sprüth Magers, saw their turnover (the UK term for revenue) grow, while others, like Hauser & Wirth, Sadie Coles HQ, and Pace, saw it drop. There was no one-size-fits-all story for the UK market in 2025.

ARTnews pulled the filings for 10 of these galleries to get a sense of how the trade is doing.

Pace’s 2025 report showed that its international business posted a $5.6 million loss in 2025. The figures cover The Pace Gallery Limited, the London-registered company that operates the gallery’s London space and owns its subsidiaries in Hong Kong, Beijing, Seoul, Geneva, and Berlin. They do not include Pace’s US or Tokyo operations.

Turnover fell 2.6 percent, from $67.7 million in 2024 to $65.9 million in 2025. Meanwhile, cost of sales rose 12 percent, gross profit dropped $7.4 million to $12.8 million, and year-end cash on hand fell from $34.8 million in 2023 to $24.1 million in 2024 and $11.1 million in 2025.

CEO Marc Glimcher told ARTnews that the gallery is “all off the bottom” and said it had a record performance at Art Basel Paris in October, though he did not offer specifics.

“We’ve done a lot of internal reengineering of the way the companies work together. The successes we’ve had in Berlin and Japan have been very, very instructive, and we have had an extremely profitable year already in Los Angeles,” Glimcher said. “The things we’ve done are already bearing fruit, and they’re bearing fruit because the market has substantially changed.”

Lisson’s 2025 financial year ended on January 31, 2026. In the filing for its parent company, Art Holding Co. Limited, the group reported a 9 percent increase in turnover, to $130 million (£97 million) from $119.42 million (£89 million) in 2024.

The group described the period as a “year of encouragement despite the wider art market continuing to face many macro-economic driven challenges.” The gallery attributed its recovery to “a couple of challenging years coupled with a renewed focus on stock and secondary sales activities.” Lisson added in the filing that the risks and uncertainties facing the business continue to relate to “inherent volatility in the contemporary art market,” and that it mitigates that risk “as far as possible by offering work from a diverse spread of artists across a wide price spectrum to a broad range of private and institutional collectors, both in the UK and internationally.”

A spokesperson for Lisson told ARTnews that while the audit shows a decrease in profit for both Lisson Gallery London Limited and Art Holding Co. Limited, Lisson’s global gross profit has increased six percent year-on-year and the losses were largely due to non-trading foreign exchange movements.

“Lisson has been able to maintain this and recover efficiently due to a number of factors, including a renewed focus on secondary sales activities and securing distribution fees (despite significant upward inflationary pressures on freight costs),” said the spokesperson.

Hauser & Wirth’s turnover fell 13.1 percent, from $90.82 million (£68.29 million) in 2024 to $78.93 million (£59.35 million) in 2025. However, the company remained profitable in 2025, with profit up 51 percent year on year, totalling £403,318 profit for 2025 against 2024’s £266,539. In the filing, the company said its directors “have a strong belief in the future of the company and are pleased to report continuing profitability during a period of art market fluctuations.”

In the filing, the gallery also noted that the UK “represented a small element of the annual program in 2025,” with nine exhibitions and two art fair presentations there, compared with 58 exhibitions and 13 fair presentations worldwide. At Frieze London and Frieze Masters in 2025, the gallery sold just under $21 million worth of works.

“As a global business, the UK company’s results are not indicative of the gallery’s overall performance, which includes larger markets such as Switzerland and the US,” a Hauser & Wirth spokesperson told ARTnews. “The gallery has a strong commitment to the UK, reflected in the major project underway to create a new London flagship on South Audley Street in Mayfair. 2026 has been a year of significant growth and investment for the gallery globally, including new spaces in Palo Alto, the Hauser & Wirth Publishers HQ in Zurich and Stockwell House the community-led space in Somerset as well as five new artists and estates joining the roster.”

At Goodman Gallery, which has locations in Johannesburg, Cape Town, New York, and London, turnover for the UK business rose 7 percent in 2025 to $47.3 million (£35.26 million), while pre-tax profit soared 60.8 percent to $6.37 million (£4.75 million). Cost of sales fell 2.3 percent to $31.95 million (£23.82 million).

“We anticipate healthier financial performance in the 2026/2027 financial year,” Liza Essers, owner and director of Goodman Gallery, told ARTnews.

The gallery is celebrating its 60th year in business, and the anniversary has helped drive sales, according to Essers. She added that the gallery’s most recent William Kentridge exhibition, which opened in September in London, has “surpassed expectations,” with films selling for $485,000 and works on paper priced from $250,000 to $850,000. Essers noted that the gallery had a strong showing at Art Basel Paris, including several significant sales to long-term clients from Europe, North America, and Asia. This year the gallery also launched Goodman Gallery Advisory, a secondary-market arm focused on 20th-century artists ranging from Alexander Calder to Yayoi Kusama.

Pilar Corrias saw its turnover fall 42.7 percent, from $25.76 million (£19.2 million) in 2024 to $14.75 million (£10.99 million) in 2025.

In the filing, the gallery said its main challenges were supply chain issues, market volatility, digital security, logistics such as shipping, the recoverability of debts, and foreign currency fluctuations. Looking ahead, the gallery said that for 2026 and beyond it would focus on reaching more collectors worldwide by showing at major international art fairs, investing in digital infrastructure to grow its online presence and improve security, and strengthening its relationships with private collectors, institutions, and museums.

The gallery did not respond to a request for comment.

Monika Sprüth & Philomene Magers Limited, the holding company of Sprüth Magers gallery, returned sharply to profitability in 2025, reporting a pre-tax profit of $1.83 million (£1.36 million) after a $2.34 million (£1.75 million) pre-tax loss in 2024. Turnover rose 66.2 percent to $24.77 million (£18.46 million).

The accounts also broke down turnover by region. UK turnover more than doubled, to $139,047 (£103,643) from $63,938 (£47,689) in 2024. Turnover from Europe rose 74.1 percent to $17.31 million (£12.9 million), while turnover from outside Europe rose 49.3 percent to $7.32 million (£5.45 million).

“Based on the performance in 2025 and current trading, the directors consider the company to be in a strong financial position as it enters 2026,” the filing said. “The outlook for 2026 is positive and the directors expect a similar level of performance to 2025, while recognising that results remain sensitive to market conditions and the timing of high-value transactions.”

The gallery did not respond to a request for comment.

Sadie Coles HQ’s turnover fell 10 percent in 2025 to $34.63 million (£25.81 million), but the gallery’s pre-tax profit rose 57.2 percent, from $536,279 (£399,731) in 2024 to $843,063 (£628,401).

“Careful curation of the gallery programme and the addition of new represented artists means that the company is continuing to attract new collectors and to expand its business,” the gallery said in the filing. It noted that turnover was slightly lower than in 2024, despite a significant increase in the total number of sales.

In fall 2025, Sadie Coles HQ opened a new space on Savile Row, which the gallery said has helped it “attract new artists of calibre.” The gallery added that it “is confident of continued success.”

Timothy Taylor reported turnover of $23 million (£17.21 million) in 2025, up 3.7 percent from $22.26 million (£16.59 million) in 2024. Cost of sales rose 5.9 percent to $17.4 million (£12.96 million), while gross profit fell 2.5 percent to $5.68 million (£4.24 million). In the filing, the gallery said it “intends to continue strengthening its brand presence in the UK, the US and Asia.”

The gallery did not respond to a request for comment.

2025 marked Thaddaeus Ropac’s ninth year of trading in the UK, and the gallery’s founder recently told ARTnews that he had renewed its lease on Dover Street for another 10 years. The gallery’s 2025 turnover fell 4.9 percent to $46.58 million (£34.72 million), while pre-tax profit fell 7.3 percent to $3.32 million (£2.47 million).

In the filing, the gallery said that 2025, like 2024, reflected “uncertainties around economy and sociopolitical upheavals,” but that it remained “profitable in this climate, a reflection of its strong engagement with its customers and artist and close control over costs.”

The gallery’s UK staff grew from 23 in 2024 to 25 in 2025. That year, Thaddaeus Ropac also opened a space in Milan, adding to its locations in London, Paris, Salzburg, and Seoul.

According to David Zwirner’s 2025 filing with Companies House, the gallery’s turnover rose 56 percent, from $49.72 million (£37.13 million) in 2024 to $77.51 million (£57.89 million) in 2025. The gallery attributed the $27.79 million (£20.8 million) jump in sales revenue to “increased art fair sales as well as revenue recognition timing.”

At the 2025 edition of Frieze London, the gallery reported sales led by a Chris Ofili painting for $700,000. It also sold a painting by Steven Shearer for $550,000, two paintings by Lucas Arruda priced from $320,000 to $350,000 each, a work on paper by Elizabeth Peyton for $300,000, a work on paper by Lisa Yuskavage for $180,000, and two works by Wolfgang Tillmans priced from $115,000 to $250,000. The gallery also sold works by Kerry James Marshall, Christopher Williams, Huma Bhabha, Sosa Joseph, and Frank Walter for undisclosed five-figure sums.

The gallery did not respond to a request for comment.
