Do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate plan. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

For most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

Yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Review your estate plan every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a new state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more important than for conventional retirees.

Estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate plan: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

#8987. John Tree forms sculptural Hoop lamp from pine for Vaarni

Designer John Tree has created the monolithic Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni, combining an “almost brutalistic block of solid pine” with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer.

Vaarni, which is known for its pine furniture and accessories, used Finnish pine from a sustainably managed forest for the lamp.

Tree‘s design for the light, which was made locally in Jurva, Finland, combines two different pieces of pine to create a sculptural shape.

“One is this heavy, almost brutalistic block of solid pine that forms a stable structural element through which a single cut is made to support the second element – a hoop of thin veneer which forms a diffuser and allows light to come through in an almost magical way,” he told Dezeen.

The hoop has an integrated light source to create a diffused glow, with Tree basing the thickness of the pine used on its ability to let the light through.

The designer also let the materials lead the way when it came to the size of the shade.

“It was in some ways an exercise in reducing the two elements to their simplest geometric forms, yet governed very much by what material would allow,” he said.

“For example, we discovered that if the thin veneer hoop became any bigger, it started to distort under its own weight,” he continued.

“Thickening it was not an option, as this stopped light from going through so we naturally arrived at an optimum form defined by the material.”

While Tree has worked with pine before, he said he hasn’t previously had the opportunity to explore the material’s properties to the extent he did for this project.

“The expertise that Vaarnii have with this material meant that we could do some very precise and complex technical details,” Tree said.

“It was interesting to see how much a material can be elevated with care and precision in its manufacture,” he continued.

“Hoop is a little celebration of pine, a humble material that can do some amazing things.”

Vaarni has previously showcased “brutal and sophisticated” furniture at 3 Days of Design and designed a chair and footstool with Faye Toogood.

#8986. Nip Slip? The Ultimate Guide to Inverted Nipples

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

The Evercade Nexus is the best version of what Evercade has been building towards. It’s comfortable, well-made, and easy to use, and it comes with a big screen, twin sticks, and the full cartridge library from day one. Banjo-Kazooie in the box shows what it can do in 3D, while the 8-bit and 16-bit classics that built the brand are still right at home. An easy recommendation.

Big, bright screen that makes 3D and mid-90s pixel art look crisp

Banjo-Kazooie bundled in the box, with native widescreen, 60fps and Stop ’n’ Swop content

Plays the entire existing Evercade games library

EverSync lets a second Nexus play a game from just one cartridge

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Controls: D-pad, face buttons, twin analogue sticks, bumpers and triggers

Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth audio, 3.5mm

Evercade Nexus is the retro game brand cracking its knuckles, stretching and embracing an even larger catalogue of retro games. Evercade has established itself as the easy entry point to retro gaming. It’s the antidote to wasting afternoons lost to getting ROMs running and fiddling with settings, and as much as I love ways to play like the Sinclair Gamer Card, I also enjoy the ease of Evercade’s cart approach, and I’ve been a fan since the first Evercade EXP.

With the Nexus, we have a retro game console that can play all the existing properly licensed games in the Evercade library, with authentic emulation and physical cartridges that scratch the collector itch, while ushering us into a ‘new’ 3D era. You pop a cart in, and you play.

So this is 'next gen', then, in the most Evercade way, with new cartridge collections stretching up to around 1998, proper 3D alongside the pixels, and a handheld that looks and feels like it belongs in 2026. I got my first hands-on with the console at the Nexus community launch in September, where I got to play Doom and Banjo-Kazooie, and I also got context for Nexus, as the room was lined with old Evercade consoles leading up to this moment. You can find many of these in our best retro consoles guide.

First thing to know: the Nexus is much bigger than the Evercade EXP and the newer EXP-R and can feel a little chunky compared to the older model. The Nexus is a proper handheld in the vein of the Nintendo Switch, not a jacket-pocket gadget. That said, the Nexus is still smaller and lighter than a Nintendo Switch 2; for context, it’s about the size of the Switch 2 display, and I've been happy playing for hours at a time.

The design has some fun touches you expect from a Sony console. The rear grips feature a subtle mesh of raised 'A' symbols that nod to the Evercade logo, and the textured rubber pads sit where your hands land to keep it from shifting. For me, and even though I love it, the Switch 2 can feel slippery in handheld mode, as its slimmer design and smaller, curved finger bridges can be too subtle. The Nexus doesn't move in the hand; it’s bulkier, yes, but also more solid in the grip.

Up front is the 5.89-inch IPS display, with controls arranged around it as you expect from a modern handheld. Evercade has opted for symmetrical analogue sticks rather than the Xbox and Nintendo offset layout, and I'm a fan. It feels closer to a PlayStation pad, and it suits 3D games well while also making 2D games easy to play.

Under the display, you get a quad-core 1.5GHz processor, 512MB of RAM, and 4GB of storage, plus Wi-Fi 6 for system updates. The 5,000mAh battery lasts more than five hours and charges via USB-C. You also get Bluetooth headphone support, a 3.5mm jack and front-facing stereo speakers.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The D-pad, you see, is also symmetrically placed opposite the face buttons, but it’s also a big step up from the older EXP's pad. It's light and responsive, which is exactly what you want for fighting games, and I've sunk plenty of time into King of the Fighters 2002 on it, and it's still going well. Switching to the classic controls for the new Atari collections feels natural, too.

The buttons are a touch clicky and light; they don't have the premium feel of pricier handhelds. Next to a Switch 2, you can see where the money went. At this price, and for the games it’s designed to play, from Doom to Activision Decathlon, that's fair, and the controls never distract.

The screen is the Nexus's biggest upgrade and one reason for its size, because embracing 3D and the more complex pixel art of games from the mid-90s onward demands a larger screen. It's a 5.89-inch IPS panel at 840 x 512, rated at over 500 nits. It isn't OLED, so don't expect the deep blacks of a premium handheld, but I came away impressed. Colours pop, contrast is solid and older games look crisp without losing their grit. The simulated CRT and other retro game effects on many cartridges sit nicely, too.

Banjo-Kazooie comes bundled in the box, and it's a brilliant showcase. Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie both get new native ports with widescreen support, higher resolution and 60fps, and that second analogue stick transforms how they play. These aren't old N64 ROMs run through an emulator. They've been nicely reworked, with modern control options and Stop 'n' Swop content. It's one of the best reasons to buy the Nexus and joins the likes of the recent Croc 2 remaster in showing how these old 3D platfomers can be improved on new hardware..

The display keeps up with faster games, too. I've been flipping between the new DOOM and DOOM II collection and the SNK titles on the new Neo Geo Arcade 4 cartridge I always drift back to because Metal Slug 4 is just too good, and the Nexus handles both. Twin sticks make DOOM feel far more natural than a D-pad ever could, and placing them symmetrically works wonders.

TATE mode is back as well, rotating the screen for vertical arcade games. The Nexus's larger size makes this mode easier to use, as I often found the Evercade EXP a little too narrow to be comfortable. The Nexus's bulk makes it a tad better than the Switch 2 for TATE mode, as I found when playing the Toaplan Arcade Garage: Flying Fire Shark; Nintendo’s console can be too slim for its own good.

The Nexus is only half the story, of course, because Evercade's physical games are the main draw, and the new handheld plays the entire existing library: more than 80 cartridges and over 700 officially licensed games from Atari, Capcom, Taito, SNK, Rare, Activision and more. Each collection arrives in its own box with a full-colour manual, and building a shelf of them is a joy a digital storefront can't match.

No downloads, no games vanishing from a subscription service, no hunting for ROMs in dodgy corners of the internet. Cart in, game on. It's refreshing and plays into the idea of celebrating how we play and not just what we play, and by plan or by accident. Evercade has become the zeitgeist brand, treating gaming like a vinyl collection.

The Nexus also debuts EverSync, a local wireless multiplayer feature. Only one player needs the cartridge; the second console receives the game from the first. It's clever, and it makes owning physical games feel more flexible and inclusive, but it also reminds me of how we used to play back in the day, when you’d share games and play on the couch. You'll need a second Nexus, though, so maybe part of Evercade is happy playing by 2026’s rules.

Two omissions stand out. The big one is HDMI. The original Evercade EXP had a Mini HDMI port; the Nexus is strictly a handheld. You can't plug it into a TV or use it as a portable home console like some rivals.

I get why. Evercade already has the VS and VS-R for TV play, and there's a business case for keeping the products apart. It's still a shame if you want one device to do everything.

The other gap is a proper sleep mode. There's no suspend and resume, so you power down and restart every time you put it away. That feels odd on a modern handheld, especially if you're used to picking up a Switch and jumping straight back in. Boot times aren't speedy either, at around 40 seconds (I know, we're in such a low attention span era, how did I survive ZX Spectrum tape-loading?), so I'd love to see a fix in a future update.

Neither is a deal-breaker. Both remind me that the Nexus is a focused console, and Evercade has clearly balanced features and specs to make it affordable.

Yes, if you want retro gaming without the faff. The Evercade Nexus is the best version of what Evercade has been building towards: comfortable, well-made, with a big screen and a huge library of classics from day one that's dead easy to play.

I like that Evercade hasn't pushed the hardware too far. Banjo-Kazooie shows what the Nexus can do in 3D, and the 8-bit and 16-bit games that built the brand are still right at home.

At $199.99 / £169.99 for the base console ($229.99 / £189.99 for the 64 Edition and $249.99 / £199.99 for the Doom Edition), it isn't competing with cheap emulation handhelds, and it's not directly competitive with Switch 2. The lack of OLED, HDMI and sleep mode will put some people off, but those are clearly choices made to keep Nexus affordable and dodge a headlong fight with Nintendo.

Evercade is selling something different: a curated, licensed, and collectable way to play some of the best games from past arcade and console eras. If you already own cartridges because you have an EXP-R or VS-R, the bigger screen and twin sticks make this a tempting upgrade. If you're new, it's still an easy recommendation.

#8984. hurricane-proof polycarbonate wraps resilient 24-hour public library in miami

faced with the challenge of sheltering an automated 24-hour library from hurricanes, the design utilizes an ambiguous, geometric steel frame wrapped entirely in high-velocity polycarbonate paneling.

Julio C. Perez edited by christina vergopoulou November 5, 2026 3 min

Designed by 89th Studio, Le Petite Bibliothèque is a 264-sqft civic shelter sited in North Miami’s Claude Pepper Park, adjacent to the Joe Celestin Recreation Center. Developed to house an automated 24-hour lending library kiosk manufactured by Ohio-based company Envisionware, whose standard modular prototypes had previously failed to meet South Florida’s High Velocity Hurricane Zone (HVHZ) building codes, the project resolves severe wind-load compliance through a bespoke, climate-responsive envelope engineered to withstand Category 5 storms.

The structure by 89th Studio is framed in structural steel with welded and mechanically fastened connections, forming a multi-gabled geometric silhouette that acts as a visual signifier within the park. To avoid the cost and weight of impact-resistant glass, the enclosure utilizes high-velocity-rated polycarbonate panels divided into two functional zones by a horizontal steel stiffener. The placement of this datum is calculated against lowest seasonal sun angles, blocking direct solar glare from the automated interface screens. The upper zone features opaque panels that reduce solar heat gain and double as interchangeable surfaces for public announcements, while the transparent lower perimeter provides direct sightlines into the kiosk to support passive security during unmonitored night hours. Fastened using standard Florida residential storm shutter track hardware to utilize local fabrication labor and reduce costs, the dual-performance skin reverses its function after dark, diffusing interior fixture light outward to establish a luminous profile across the park.

the building’s profile shifts from a series of distinct geometric shapes into a singular cohesive objectmulti-wall polycarbonate paneling replaces conventional, heavy impact glass

#8982. Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

So… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

#8981. Sabine Marcelis takes a moment to reflect in first museum exhibition

Photography by Umberto Romito and Ivan Šuta

Sabine Marcelis has a knack for creating viral objects, from IKEA’s most-sold light to her mesmerising Candy Cube tables. Now, the designer is revealing the method behind her “magic” in an exhibition at Zürich‘s Museum für Gestaltung.

Light and Color is the first museum show dedicated entirely to Marcelis‘s work since she founded her studio 15 years ago.

In that time, the Rotterdam-based Kiwi has gone from being a student at the Design Academy Eindhoven to one of the most prolific and in-demand designers working today.

“This is the first time a museum has brought so much of my work together in one place,” Marcelis told Dezeen. “I’m always so preoccupied with what’s next that I don’t like to look back so much, but it’s amazing to have this moment to actually stop and look back for a minute.”

The show brings together 17 key pieces from the last decade and a half, going as far back as Tall Stripe – the first of many mirrors – and her signature resin Candy Cubes, which first catapulted the designer to international acclaim in 2014.

But Marcelis is adamant it should not be considered a retrospective.

“I didn’t want the show to feel like a retrospective in the sense of a chronological archive,” she said. “I wanted to select a variety of projects that each show a different way of working with light and colour.”

Rather than chronologically, the exhibits are arranged by colour, blending into each other like the soft gradients she favours in works like her curved glass chaise longues for the Barcelona Pavilion.

Her favourite materials – glass, resin and stone – recur throughout the exhibition, with carefully placed spotlights showing off the play of reflections and shadows the designer has learned to elicit through years of experimentation.

A prime example is her Lokum coffee table for Acerbis, stacked on top of each other on a curved wall to show the gradients of colour and water-like reflections created when the glass is seen at different angles and levels of illumination.

There are also two room-scale installations, reminiscent of Yayoi Kusama‘s Infinity Mirror Rooms, throwing back endless reflections of Marcelis’s viral IKEA “donut lamp” and the towering three-metre-tall Column lava lamp for Mathmos.

For the show’s curator Damian Fopp, these are less about Instagram bait and more about allowing visitors to experience the full visual effect of these objects in real life, rather than through a screen.

“Her work circulated widely as images, but no institution had looked at it as a whole,” he said. “This also made it interesting to shift the conversation back from online to physical.”

“And we wanted to show what lies behind those calm, effortless images: the testing, prototyping and production that I discovered when I visited her studio in Rotterdam.”

A mini-documentary and a book commissioned for the exhibition pull back the curtain on what it takes to create these perception-bending pieces with her team.

Over the years, these have become more ambitious in scale as well as sustainability, pivoting to 99 per cent biobased resin for her production and creating installations for the likes of Coachella and Apple HQ,

But no matter the size of the project, Marcelis says that materials remain her North Star.

“I wrote a one-sentence summary of what my studio does ten years ago,” she remembered. “‘A studio for material, installation and object design. Forever in search of magical moments within materiality and manufacturing processes to create unexpected experiences.'”

“I wouldn’t change that sentence today if I had to make the same summary again.”

Photography by Umberto Romito and Ivan Šuta

#8979. architecture that invites nature as a designer, from dissolving walls to insect-built pavilions

these built spaces invite natural forces into the design process, allowing materials to dissolve and buildings to change.

On South Korea’s Jeju Island, architecture studio stpmj built a small arch from rose-colored salt bricks, knowing that the island’s summer rainfall would eventually dissolve it. Over several months, the solid masonry gradually disappeared, leaving a delicate framework of mortar in its place. The weather had effectively been given permission to redesign the building.

Architecture typically seeks to control the natural forces around it, keeping water outside and protecting materials against decay. Yet a number of experimental structures propose a different relationship, allowing these conditions to become active participants in the design process.

From pavilions shaped by desert winds to structures constructed by insects, these seven projects explore what happens when architects give the environment a say in how their buildings take shape.

The walls of Dissolving Arch were always intended to disappear. Installed at the Osulloc Tea Museum on Jeju Island, the compact vault was built from translucent rock-salt bricks joined by cement mortar. Its pink masonry initially enclosed a narrow passageway, filtering daylight through the material before the island’s rainy season began to change its appearance.

The architects at stpmj deliberately chose materials with different reactions to water. While the salt bricks dissolved under repeated rainfall and humidity, the mortar remained, gradually revealing an open lattice where solid walls once stood. Over the exhibition period, the arch became more porous, admitting light and views of the surrounding landscape. Its final appearance emerged through the island’s weather, with rain completing a process that the architects had set in motion.

Amber-colored and almost glasslike, Neri Oxman‘s Aguahoja I rises five meters in a series of translucent surfaces that vary in thickness and flexibility. Developed by the designer together with the Mediated Matter Group at MIT, the pavilion was robotically fabricated from biopolymers derived from organic sources, including cellulose and chitosan. Its material composition allows it to respond to environmental exposure in ways conventional building materials are generally designed to resist.

Over time, the biopolymers can break down when exposed to water, allowing the structure to gradually return to the environment. When the original pavilion was later installed on an outdoor terrace at SFMOMA, researchers used instruments to monitor its exposure to the elements and study its decomposition. The project considers the eventual disappearance of architecture as part of its design, with the material’s lifespan considered from the beginning.

Winter temperatures became the principal building tool for Curtain, a temporary shelter installed on Winnipeg’s frozen Assiniboine River. Designed by Alejandro Felix and Fang Cui, the pavilion began with a simple timber framework wrapped in ropes. Water pumped from beneath the river ice was directed through a dripping system, allowing icicles to form along the suspended strands.

As the water continued freezing, ice accumulated into thick, irregular walls, gradually turning the open framework into an enclosed shelter. The process worked in reverse as temperatures rose. The icy surfaces thinned and became increasingly translucent before openings appeared and the timber structure emerged again.

Throughout the winter, the pavilion changed with the weather, its enclosure growing and disappearing according to the temperature outside.

Curtain, Alejandro Felix and Fang Cui, Winnipeg, Canada 2023Curtain, Alejandro Felix and Fang Cui, Winnipeg, Canada 2023

A bright-yellow steel ring now occupies the tidal Schuylkill River near Bartram’s Garden in Philadelphia. Known as FloatLab, the 75-foot-wide structure was developed by J. Meejin Yoon and Höweler + Yoon Architecture to rise and fall with changing water levels through a buoyancy and ballast system.

The river’s daily tidal cycle, which can produce fluctuations of approximately five to seven feet, determines the structure’s elevation. Its sloping circular walkway is designed to bring visitors toward the water’s surface while keeping them within the structure. FloatLab has arrived at its Philadelphia site, with public access planned for spring 2027.

Here, the architecture enters into a continuous relationship with a moving body of water, allowing the tides to govern its position throughout the day.

Strong desert winds supplied much of the final geometry for Ghost House, an installation by architecture studio i/thee in California’s Morongo Valley. The project began with two lightweight timber frames outlining the familiar shapes of small houses. Custom-cut canvas sheets, soaked in a water-based adhesive, were draped over the structures and left exposed to the mountain winds.

Over several hours, the fabric billowed and twisted before the adhesive hardened, fixing its windblown shapes in place. Square openings were subsequently cut into the surfaces, giving the sculptural forms the suggestion of windows.

The completed structures capture the atmospheric conditions of a particular moment, their irregular enclosures shaped by gusts moving through the site during construction. The architects established the framework, while the wind determined much of the finished geometry.

The bright-yellow canopies of Puddle Pavilion began as pools of liquid material spreading across the ground. For the installation beside Mud Creek in Bondurant, Iowa, architecture studio i/thee poured algae-based bio-resin directly onto a flat surface, allowing gravity and surface tension to influence its shape without conventional molds.

Once the resin had hardened, the irregular sheets were lifted onto slender steel columns, turning the flattened puddles into elevated architectural canopies. Their undulating edges and varying thicknesses preserve the behavior of the liquid during casting.

The architects controlled where the material was introduced, while its movement across the ground helped determine the finished geometry. What began as a flowing substance now hovers above the landscape, holding the shape it acquired before solidifying.

Some 17,532 silkworms participated in the construction of Silk Pavilion II, a six-meter-tall structure developed by Neri Oxman and the Mediated Matter Group. The insects were introduced onto a specially designed textile supported by a steel framework, where they spun layers of silk that became part of the architectural enclosure.

During fabrication, a rotating apparatus helped guide the silkworms across the surface, while changes in light and temperature influenced their movements and the density of the silk they produced. Their biological processes also affected the underlying fabric, creating openings within the finished enclosure.

Presented as part of a larger exhibition at New York’s Museum of Modern Art (see here), the pavilion combines human-designed infrastructure with a material surface physically produced by another species.

Across these seven experiments, architecture becomes something that can continue changing beyond the designer’s initial intervention. Rain gradually removes a wall, while freezing water constructs another. Elsewhere, the behavior of liquid materials or passing winds determines the shape of a structure before it is complete.

With Silk Pavilion II, the question extends to the construction process itself, where architects establish the conditions for another living organism to contribute to the finished work. The building becomes a collaboration, with its final form determined by more than the person who drew it.

#8978. Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

The creative possibilities are endless if you know how to approach it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With a whole spectrum of colours only a few clicks away, perhaps it’s not surprising that working in black and white is sometimes overlooked.

But whether you’re working monochromatically to draft an illustration or using it for a finished piece, a black and white approach is full of benefits. It can even make you stand out in an art world that's saturated with vibrant talent (if you need the tools for your own art, see our guides to the best drawing tablets and the best pens for artists).

Foregoing colour can be an intentional creative choice rather than the result of a limitation, but for illustrator Sarah Koudelka-Mason it was born out of convenience. “After trying out all sorts of tools, I found pencils to be the simplest, least fussy medium,” she says. “All you need is a pencil and paper, which you can bring anywhere. Perhaps because pencils were also my first and most consistent tool in my art journey, I feel the most comfortable with them.”

For character artist and illustrator Joe Vriens, a black and white approach was the result of a fear of colour theory mixed with a dash of impatience.

“I’d always get excited to see the bare line work of a comic, too; it seemed much more achievable,” he reveals. “I could grab a pen and paper and make a comic without expensive markers, paints or digital tools.

“I’m also old enough to remember King Kong in black and white. I made my parents rent that thing probably once a month. In retrospect, maybe King Kong informed my approach all along?”

Illustrator Isabella Mazzanti points out that working in black and white plays into a long tradition of art styles, including her own influences which range from Gustave Doré’s engravings to contemporary manga.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

“They seemed accessible and reproducible to me,” she says. “These early experiences were fundamental, because they shaped my aesthetic sensibility and my approach to drawing.”

Seeing as working in black in white is a deliberate approach, it also depends on specific considerations.

“You have to make sure the shading values are balanced well,” Sarah advises. “It’s easy for your shading to look flat or ’muddy’ if your tones are too similar, so you really have to figure out your darks, mediums and lights, and then tie them together with the between shading. I personally like to work lighter and work my way to the crisp dark lines at the end. So satisfying.”

“Line weight and shape design are also key,” says concept artist Alexander Joseba, who has worked for Epic Games, HBO, Ubisoft and more. “A strong silhouette can communicate a character or object very quickly, and different line weights can help separate forms and create depth. Since you cannot use colour to separate materials or planes, you need to do it through values, textures, edges and rhythm.”

“For me, black and white forces you to be more disciplined, although I also like to play with a more wild and instinctive approach. If the image works in black and white, it usually means that the composition, lighting and structure are solid.”

Alexander grew up looking at the work of great artists such as John Buscema, Mike Mignola, Alberto Breccia and many others.

“I was fascinated by the way they were able to communicate so much with ink: how they separated planes, created depth, controlled light and shadow, and made the whole image work so clearly, each one with their own very distinct style,” he explains

Some extra considerations are required when working in black and white, however. Alexander believes the most important consideration is readability.

“Without colour, you have to rely much more on values, contrast, shapes, silhouettes and composition to guide the viewer’s eye. Everything needs to be clear from the beginning: what the focal point is, what belongs to the foreground, middle ground and background, and where the main light is coming from.

“Working in black and white forces you to focus on the foundation of the image. You need to solve composition, lighting, values, silhouette, volume and overall readability properly. I think any artist who works well in black and white will also improve their colour work, because they understand values, light and structure better. Colour does not replace that foundation; it complements it.”

Isabella also warns against assuming that working in black and white is a simpler approach.

“A solid grasp of the visual language is essential in order to use it effectively,” she argues. “Black and white is not simply the absence of colour; when working with chiaroscuro, one chooses to tell a story based on duality, contrast and the exaggeration of ambiguity. I believe it is vitally important for an artist to understand this element, which has the power to intensify the viewer’s emotional engagement.”

When it comes to making black and white art work professionally, Isabella stresses that economic forces may be influencing publishers just as much as aesthetic considerations. “It lends images a classic, refined and timeless quality,” she says.

“Even when telling a certain type of story – for example, Gothic literature – black and white seems to be the most natural choice. It can be a risky choice, because one is foregoing the emotional appeal of colour, but when used in the right way and in the right context, it’s a winning decision.”

Sarah claims that black and white art is underrated, and that it’s not the usual approach commissioners are looking for. “But at the same time, if there are clients specifically looking for works of that nature and you’ve established yourself in that niche, you will find them. This applies to any unique niche of art, and I personally enjoy the challenge of going against the grain!”

For Alexander, black and white artwork is useful for both commercial production pipelines and for final illustration styles. “It depends on the project: sometimes it is a practical development tool, and sometimes it becomes the final artistic language,” he says.

Even if artists don’t gear their black and white artwork towards clients, focusing on it can still improve their overall craft. “Balancing tones in a final image is super-important, so if you can master greys then moving on to colour will feel easier,” says Joe.

“You can guide the viewer’s eye with tones alone, so it can help your compositions greatly. Focusing on greys or even black and white can take a lot of the pressure off as well, which allows you to really dig into lighting and form.”

Meanwhile Sarah is a firm believer that practising black and white art is one of the best ways to strengthen your understanding of the fundamentals.

“Without the distraction or support of vibrant colours, you are encouraged to look at your work in a simpler and more intentional way,” she says. “You start to see shape language, values, lighting, contrast, composition and depth a lot clearer.

Isabella agrees: “The absence of colour changes the way an image is perceived,” she says. “Rather than depriving the image of something, a black and white approach reveals its essential and most intimate nature; it speaks to the viewer in a more universal, almost archetypal language.”

#8976. Yinka Ilori reveals Tottenham Hotspur away shirt

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has collaborated with Premier League football team Tottenham Hotspur to create a customised version of the club’s colourful away shirt.

Ilori reimagined the colourful away shirt, which was designed by Nike with a pattern of “never-before-seen visuals inspired by never-before-seen destinations”, by adding a graphic to the front and back.

On the front, in the position the sponsor logo is usually located, Ilori designed a circular motif combining the football club’s initials – THFC – with an abbreviation for London and the postcode for Tottenham, LDN17.

The lettering is bright orange with a white background.

On the rear of the shirt, Ilori created a graphic in his typical playful style around the letters COYS, which stands for Come On You Spurs.

Encircling the letters are the words “I know I am, I’m sure I am”, with the words “We are Tottenham wherever we go” around the whole graphic.

All of the lettering uses Ilori’s custom typeface, which was designed by type foundry British Standard Type for the designer in 2024.

According to the designer, who grew up in north London where the Populous-designed Tottenham Hotspur stadium is located, the collaboration aims to demonstrate the power of football to unite people.

“This project is a celebration of belonging and the power of football to bring people together,” said Ilori.

“For me, football is about the wider culture and the incredible sense of unity that comes from standing on the terraces, chanting alongside thousands of others,” he continued.

“I wanted the design to honour Tottenham Hotspur’s heritage while capturing that collective joy and spirit. The ‘Never Far From Home’ message really resonated with me, reflecting how football has the power to make you feel at home, wherever you are.”

The shirt is the latest design from the designer who has recently collaborated with brands including Brabantia and Veuve Clicquot.

Ilori also recently created a homeware and furniture collection for department store Dunelm.

#8975. Extra Skin? 9 Exercises for A Sagging Neck

We’re not in love with the term “turkey neck” — it’s just extra skin.

If you don’t want to learn to love the extra chin you’re in (though we wish you would!), you can perform some exercises that may tighten your neck muscles.

Though some swear these moves work, there’s no research backing them up, and they can’t zap away extra flowy skin.

Instead, they’re more likely to help strengthen the muscles underneath loose neck skin. Unfortunately, skin removal is usually accomplished with more intense methods, like surgery.

However, these popular neck exercises are simple enough for a test drive and may help tone your neck muscles naturally.

Exercise may be possible to tighten up a turkey neck, but it doesn’t eliminate loose skin like surgery or lasers.

Yes. Certain cosmetic products and procedures — especially surgery — improve loose neck skin the best. These include surgical neck lifts, lasers, Botox, and certain neck creams.

Surgery and other cosmetic methods for turkey neck can offer impressive results.

Are you not into cosmetic procedures or surgery? Neck-toning exercises and facial yoga movements may offer some improvement. However, loose skin is generally not tightened naturally.

Loose neck skin is normal (and honestly v common).

Still, these simple moves may result in toned neck muscles. Just be careful so you don’t wind up with an actual pain in the neck. If you can, it’s best to chat with a healthcare professional first.

#8974. modular audio player is built using repurposed CD-ROM drives

the aluminum CD player explores ownership, repairability, and the physical experience of music.

dasPOD edited by christina vergopoulou November 6, 2026 5 min

CD-ROM PLAYER 01 by das_POD is a DIY audio project that repurposes used computer CD-ROM drives as the basis for a functional CD player. The project combines upcycling, user assembly, and long-life product design, allowing each player to be built around a separately sourced drive and a laser-cut aluminum enclosure.

The project began with a DIY tutorial demonstrating how an old CD-ROM drive could be converted into a functional CD player. This approach led das_POD to explore a new interpretation based on the reuse of existing computer hardware instead of manufacturing a completely new CD mechanism. The sourcing process forms part of the project. Used CD-ROM drives are selected through platforms such as eBay, with different models compared according to their production year, manufacturer, mechanical construction, and appearance.

The selection of the drive therefore becomes one of the variables that distinguishes each finished player. The approach draws on a broader culture of upcycling in which existing objects are given new functions while retaining traces of their previous use. References include vintage mountain bikes, classic cars, military surplus, the original Air Jordan 1, and brands such as Freitag, where the history and continued use of an object contribute to its value.

CD-ROM PLAYER 01 is supplied by das_POD as a kit instead of a completed product. Users select their own CD-ROM drive before assembling the player, allowing the final object to reflect the characteristics of the chosen hardware. The kit contains laser-cut aluminum panels and electronic components. Users bend and assemble the panels, install the selected CD-ROM drive, connect the electronics, and construct the player themselves. The process exposes the internal structure and operation of the device, providing a practical understanding of its components and making future maintenance and repair more accessible. This construction method also makes the reused drive an integral part of the design. Instead of concealing the origins of the hardware, the system is built around the differences between individual CD-ROM models.

The enclosure is manufactured from laser-cut aluminum panels designed by das_POD studio to be assembled into the final structure. The flat components are transformed through bending and assembly into a functional housing for the drive and electronics. The enclosure is available in three finishes: Natural Anodized, Orange Powder Coat, and Matte Black Powder Coat. The anodized version retains the appearance of aluminum while using shot blasting and anodizing to increase surface durability. The powder-coated versions use a baked coating that produces a more opaque and robust surface treatment. The three finishes provide different visual treatments while maintaining the same underlying construction system. Their final forms were refined through repeated prototyping and adjustments to the enclosure and assembly process.

CD-ROM PLAYER 01 combines the reuse of obsolete computer hardware with a product architecture designed for user participation. The selected CD-ROM drive remains replaceable, while the accessible construction allows the internal components to be understood, maintained, and repaired. The project therefore shifts the CD player from a finished consumer electronic device toward an assembly system in which sourcing, construction, use, and maintenance form part of the product’s design. Its emphasis is on extending the usefulness of existing technology while giving users a direct role in constructing the object they use.

Apartment D Films’ Cami Kwan discusses the intricate process behind the handcrafted film.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The fight for the Christmas advert crown is on, and brands have set standards high this year. From hand-drawn animation to immersive storytelling, there's been a wonderful display of hand-crafted creativity, and among the ranks, beauty brand e.l.f. did not disappoint.

As the brand's first-ever holiday campaign, the beautiful stop-motion animation is a sparkling debut that captures the joy of the festive season. A masterful display of tactile craftsmanship, the 'e.l.f. Made to Stand Out' campaign carries many of the traits of the best Christmas adverts, proving that analogue storytelling is the perfect tool for sparking festive joy.

Narrated by iconic actor Alan Cumming, the campaign follows friends Kit, Echo and Cleo as they reunite in their hometown for a holiday get-together. What could be an uncomfortable hangout turns into a celebration of the qualities that make them extraordinary, spreading festive cheer.

“For a campaign about the power of standing out, the medium needed to stand out too, and stop motion felt like such a natural fit for this story," explains Oshiya Savur, chief marketing officer at e.l.f. Beauty. "We're seeing a real appetite for nostalgia and a return to simpler times, with 72% of Americans saying nostalgic memories inspire them when life feels complicated.

There's an incredible level of craftsmanship and character that comes from building an entire world by hand

There's something about stop motion that takes you right back to the holiday specials you grew up watching, but we saw an opportunity to give that familiar art form a uniquely e.l.f. twist. There's an incredible level of craftsmanship and character that comes from building an entire world by hand, and when you combine that with our signature wit and wink, you create something that feels both familiar and completely unexpected.”

Created by Apartment D Films, each element of the ad reads as a love letter to analogue craft, from individually moulded characters to intricately constructed miniature sets. "We used a wide variety of different materials! It's truly a mixed media project," Cami Kwan, Creative Director of Apartment D, tells Creative Bloq. "The puppets have aluminium and steel wire armatures inside, which makes them posable. Their hands and heads are made of printed resin, which we then painted and finished with actual e.l.f. products! The cheeks and mouths of the puppets are colored using a combination of e.l.f. Powder Blush Palette, e.l.f Perfect 10 Eyeshadow Palette, and e.l.f. Halo Glow Silky Powder Highlighter.

All the characters' hair is made with different weights and textures of yarn, to call back to super nostalgic toys, but with a modern sensibility. The eyebrows and eyelids of the characters are made of a mix of wax and clay, so they're super mouldable to get big expressions in the performance, and also so you can literally see the animators' fingerprints on the characters as they emote.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

A lot of the world around the character is made of wood, but with hand-painted textures so the wood grain is more painterly and stylized. The mini products and bottles the characters use are all hand-sculpted out of clay, and then finished with a variety of nail art techniques, like cured acrylic, gels, and powder shimmers! The mini bottles are really so, so small; none of them is more than 1 inch tall."

It wasn't a project without some difficulties, as Cami explains. "One of our challenges was integrating real beauty products intended to live on human skin with stop-motion puppets. Unlike real humans, our puppets don't have pores and don't have a body temperature, both of which e.l.f. beauty products are chemically formulated to interact with.

On top of that, stop motion puppets are designed to be handled and touched constantly during the animation process, so the treatments and colors on them need to be incredibly resilient to constant wear and tear. We spent a good deal of time on the material testing of the e.l.f. beauty products to see which ones would integrate best with our fabrication techniques.

We're seeing a renewed appreciation for the analog, and I think that's a natural response to an increasingly digital world

It was actually really interesting to let our puppet team dip into their extensive knowledge of material science! We've found that generally anything based in a powder pigment merged really well with our typical techniques, and those combinations were really successful in getting puppets with a lot of character and a lot of dynamic color and shimmer on screen!"

Honouring such a tactile animation style is a time intensive practice, but are audiences hungry for analogue creativity? “Absolutely," says Oshiya. "The more purely AI-generated content we see, the greater the opposite and equal reaction from people craving something real: human connection and creativity they can actually feel.

We're seeing a renewed appreciation for the analogue, and I think that's a natural response to an increasingly digital world. At e.l.f., we're human first, human last. AI can be an incredible tool, but taste, discernment and original ideas come from human ingenuity. At the end of the day, we want to make people feel something, and that human element is what makes it possible.”

"The thing I'm most proud of is how kind and collaborative our crew on this project was. It's not something you can point to on screen, but it's something you can feel in how much care was taken with every frame, and how lively the animation is. There was so much joy in the creation and filming of this project, and I do think you can feel that in how kinetic and inventive everything is. It's a little zany, a little imperfect, and really so captivating when all seen together!" says Cami.

Every quirk and detail adds personality to the story, and there's no expectation of perfection.

"For a more specific on-screen detail, though, I love the smear frames we used when Echo is zooming between the tables and getting everyone amped up! Smear frames are an animation technique that's most typical in 2D animation – they're moments when, for just a few frames, you distort the character and literally smear them to give a sense of speed, mimicking the way something moving too fast on a live-action camera will appear blurry.

You hardly ever see smear frames in stop motion, but one of the things that we really focus on at Apartment D is pushing the stylistic boundaries of stop motion and finding ways to bring 2D animation techniques into our three-dimensional medium. So, in that Echo zooming scene, we actually used pieces of cut paper to create practical, dimensional smear frames! Jen Prokopowicz, the animator of that shot, curved the paper smears to get an extra sense of dimension, and created smears of different sizes to get a sense of speeding up and slowing down. It's just so cool, and something that generally only real animation nerds will notice," Kami adds.

“At e.l.f., we've never been interested in being part of a sea of sameness. We're a brand that celebrates the unexpected, embraces individuality and believes that what makes us different is what makes us extraordinary. That's what I love about stop motion. Every quirk and detail adds personality to the story, and there's no expectation of perfection. Just as no two handcrafted creations are exactly alike, no two people are either. It's a playful way to bring our belief in celebrating every eye, lip and face to life, and a reminder that your difference is low-key your gift,” says Oshiya.

#8972. Nopales Benefits: Why You Might Add Cactus to Your Diet

Looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.)

Nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

Older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

You can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:

If you’re new to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

The most accessible, repeatable high-value hotel redemption in travel rewards

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: You've been grinding toward your FI number, optimizing every dollar, and you've accumulated a stash of Chase Ultimate Rewards points sitting in your account. Now imagine checking into a clean, comfortable Hyatt Place in a city you're visiting for a wedding, a family reunion, or a long weekend — and the front desk agent hands you your keycard while your account balance drops by exactly 5,000 points. Not $150. Not $180. Five thousand points that you earned by buying groceries. That's the Category 1 Hyatt sweet spot — and it's the single most accessible, repeatable, high-value redemption in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A standard night at a Hyatt Place or Hyatt House in a mid-size U.S. city routinely runs **$100–$200 per night** in cash. At 5,000 points per night, you're redeeming at **2–4 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that demolishes the standard 1 cent per point benchmark that most casual rewards users never surpass. At 4 CPP on a $200 night, you're getting four times the value of a simple cash-back card. Every. Single. Time. The pricing inefficiency here is structural, not accidental. World of Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** — meaning a Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in January or a Friday night during a sold-out college football weekend when cash rates are spiking. The loyalty program doesn't dynamically price awards the way airlines do. That fixed ceiling is your edge. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption isn't just good — it's foundational. It's the first sweet spot that proves the system works. Before you're ready to redeem 60,000 points for a business class flight to Tokyo, you need to feel what it's like to hand over a handful of points and walk into a hotel room that would have cost you real money. This is that moment. It builds the muscle memory, the confidence, and the conviction that travel rewards are real — and that you're playing the game correctly. This is where the journey starts.

World of Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value of any major hotel loyalty program. While Hilton and Marriott have moved to dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate based on demand — Hyatt maintains a fixed award chart. This structural difference is your edge. A Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it is a quiet Tuesday in February or a sold-out homecoming weekend. Combined with Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer ratios (1:1 from Sapphire Reserve, 4:3 from Sapphire Preferred) and instant transfer speed, Hyatt redemptions are the single best use of UR points for hotel stays. The ChooseFI community considers this the entry point that proves the entire travel rewards system works.

The core insight behind this sweet spot is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt uses a fixed-price award chart, and Category 1 is priced at a floor that hasn't kept pace with rising hotel cash rates.

Most hotel loyalty programs have moved to dynamic pricing — meaning award nights fluctuate with demand, just like cash rates. Marriott Bonvoy, Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards — they've all largely eliminated fixed charts in favor of algorithms that squeeze more points out of you when demand is high. Hyatt has held the line on a fixed chart, and that stubbornness is your opportunity.

The Category 1 floor sits at 5,000 points per night. As cash rates for qualifying properties have climbed with inflation — many now regularly pricing at $150–$200+ — the points cost has remained anchored. The gap between what the market charges and what Hyatt charges in points is widening in your favor every year. That's not a bug in the system. It's a feature you're uniquely positioned to exploit by understanding it.

This redemption is built on two of the best transferable points currencies available to everyday consumers:

Both transfers are instant, which means you can search for availability before committing your points, confirm the room you want is bookable, and then initiate the transfer and complete the booking — all in one sitting. This is a critical distinction from some airline partners where transfers take 24–72 hours and you're transferring on faith. With Hyatt, there's no leap of faith required.

The transfer ratio matters. With a Sapphire Reserve, every UR point becomes one Hyatt point — 15,000 UR points covers three Category 1 nights with zero waste. With a Sapphire Preferred, the 4:3 ratio means you need 20,000 UR points for the same 15,000 Hyatt points. Bilt transfers at 1:1.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award bookings. This matters more for higher-tier redemptions, but it's worth internalizing as a feature of the program overall. When you book 5,000 points for a hotel night, that's your cost. You'll pay any applicable taxes at checkout — typically $10–$25 — but there are no program-imposed carrier fees or redemption surcharges eating into your value.

Hyatt's full chart runs from 3,500 points (Category 1 standard) up to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. Understanding this structure helps you see the Category 1 sweet spot in context: it's the entry point, but it's not a consolation prize. Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties are upper-midscale hotels — clean, well-maintained, often with free breakfast at Hyatt House locations and complimentary parking in suburban markets. These aren't budget motels. You're getting a genuinely comfortable night's sleep for points that most people have already earned without trying.

Booking a Category 1 Hyatt award is one of the smoothest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's exactly how to do it from start to finish.

Before anything else, log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards or your Bilt Rewards account at biltrewards.com and confirm your current points balance. You need a minimum of 5,000 points per night to execute this redemption. If you have 15,000 points, you can book up to three nights.

Go to hyatt.com and log in or create a free World of Hyatt account (it's free to join). Use the search bar to enter your destination city and travel dates. Once results populate, filter by "Points" or "Use Points" using the toggle at the top of the results page. This will display the award rate alongside the cash rate for every property.

Filter further by selecting "Category 1–2" under the Points filter to quickly surface the lowest-cost options. Availability is typically strong — Hyatt.com shows real-time award inventory, and Category 1 properties almost always have rooms open. The booking window extends 395 days out, so you can plan well in advance for travel around a specific event.

Once you've found the property and dates you want, note the exact points cost displayed. For Category 1 properties, this should read 5,000 points per night. Add the room to your cart and proceed — but do not check out yet if your Hyatt account currently has zero balance.

Open a new browser tab and navigate to your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards) or Bilt dashboard. Select "Transfer to Travel Partners" and choose World of Hyatt from the list. Enter the number of points you need (5,000 per night, minimum), confirm your World of Hyatt membership number, and initiate the transfer.

Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant. Note: Sapphire Reserve transfers at 1:1 while Sapphire Preferred transfers at 4:3 (4 UR = 3 Hyatt). Refresh your Hyatt account and your points will be there, ready to use.

Return to your Hyatt browser tab and complete the checkout process. Select "Redeem Points" as your payment method, confirm the points deduction matches what you expected, and finalize the reservation. You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

If your preferred property shows no award availability on your dates, try these workarounds:

Go to hyatt.com and use the "Points + Cash" or "Use Points" search filter. Category 1 properties will display at 5,000 points per night. You can also browse by category directly — look for Hyatt Place and Hyatt House locations in secondary cities and suburban markets.

Always verify that your desired dates show award availability before initiating a transfer from Chase or Bilt. While transfers are instant, confirming availability first ensures you never have orphaned points sitting in your Hyatt account with no immediate use.

Log into your Chase or Bilt account, navigate to the transfer partners section, select World of Hyatt, and transfer the exact number of points needed. Transfers are instant. With a Sapphire Reserve, 5,000 UR points become 5,000 Hyatt points (1:1). With a Sapphire Preferred, you need approximately 6,700 UR points for 5,000 Hyatt points (4:3 ratio). Bilt transfers at 1:1.

Once the points land in your Hyatt account, complete the booking through hyatt.com or the World of Hyatt app. You will pay applicable taxes at checkout (typically $10 to $25 per night) but no additional redemption fees.

Before booking, note the cash rate for the same room and dates. Divide the cash rate by 5,000 to calculate your cents per point. If a room costs $150 per night and you are paying 5,000 points, you are getting 3 cents per point — triple the baseline 1 cent per point cash back value.
