Let's make this concrete. You're flying into Nashville for a long weekend — maybe it's a bachelorette party, a music festival, or just a trip you've been putting off. You pull up Hyatt.com and search Nashville for a Friday–Sunday stay (two nights).

The Hyatt Place Nashville / Brentwood shows cash rates of $169 per night — that's $338 for your two-night stay before taxes. Totally reasonable for Nashville on a weekend, but $338 is $338.

Now look at the award column: 5,000 points per night. Two nights: 10,000 points.

You transferred 10,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points from your Sapphire Reserve to World of Hyatt last week (it took about 30 seconds, and at 1:1 every point landed). Your Hyatt account shows a 10,000-point balance. You complete the booking, pay the ~$30 in taxes at checkout, and you're done.

That's more than three times the value most people extract from their points programs. And those 10,000 Chase UR points? You earned them by putting your regular monthly spending on your Chase Sapphire card for a few months.

At the Hyatt Place, you'll check into a well-appointed room with a king bed, a sofa sleating area, and a bathroom that doesn't make you feel like you're in a budget motel. Hyatt House properties (also frequently Category 1 or 2) often include a complimentary hot breakfast — eggs, waffles, fruit — served every morning. In some suburban markets, these properties also offer free parking, turning your 5,000-point night into an even stronger value play when you factor in parking rates that might otherwise run $20–$30/night.

This isn't a flashy Park Hyatt penthouse suite. But it's a genuinely comfortable, predictably high-quality stay that you've effectively taken off your cash budget — freeing that $338 for experiences, food, or your investment accounts. That's the ChooseFI mindset applied to travel.

Stack your Hyatt Globalist benefits if you qualify. If you hold World of Hyatt's top elite status (Globalist, earned at 60 qualifying nights), you receive complimentary breakfast at most full-service properties and room upgrades. Even on a 5,000-point award night, your elite benefits apply. That free breakfast alone can add $25–$35 of value to every morning.

Use the Hyatt free night award from the World of Hyatt Credit Card. The World of Hyatt Credit Card (issued by Chase) comes with an annual free night certificate valid at Category 1–4 properties. Stack this with a paid or points night to effectively get one night free on a multi-night stay — no points required.

Book as far out as you can. The Hyatt booking window opens 395 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer weekends, holiday weekends, major events — inventory at Category 1 properties can thin out. Getting in early locks your room and your rate.

Target Hyatt House properties for family trips. Hyatt House locations frequently feature suite-style rooms with full kitchens, separate living areas, and free hot breakfast included for all guests. A family of four can stay comfortably for 5,000–8,000 points and skip the cost of restaurant breakfasts entirely.

Earn points on the Bilt card on Rent Day. Bilt Rewards runs a bonus promotion on the first of each month — transferring points earned that day at elevated rates. Accumulating Bilt points through rent payments (no transaction fee) is one of the most efficient ways to build a Hyatt balance.

Don't transfer points speculatively. Even though Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant, always confirm your specific dates show award availability before transferring. Points transferred to Hyatt cannot be moved back.

Don't ignore the expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. A single qualifying activity — a points transfer, a stay, a credit card purchase — resets the clock. Set a calendar reminder annually to ensure you don't lose your balance.

Don't overlook Category 2 properties. At 8,000 points per night, Category 2 Hyatts often include urban full-service hotels that provide dramatically more value than the jump in points cost suggests. Once you're comfortable with Category 1 redemptions, explore Category 2 as a natural next step.

This redemption was built for the travel rewards beginner — the person who has accumulated their first 10,000–20,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt points and isn't yet sure if the whole system is real. It's also for the seasoned optimizer who wants a reliable, low-friction redemption they can execute on short notice.

Minimum points needed: 5,000 for a single night. Most people engaging seriously with Chase UR earning will accumulate this through normal spending in a single billing cycle.

In the broader ChooseFI travel strategy, Category 1 Hyatt nights serve as the building blocks — the reliable, repeatable foundation that funds your domestic travel while you accumulate larger balances for the aspirational redemptions.

**Difficulty Rating: Easy — and we mean it.** This is the redemption we'd hand to someone who just got their first travel rewards credit card and wants to see if the points are real. The score of 5/5 on Beginner Friendliness reflects every dimension of the experience: earning the points is straightforward, the transfer path is clear, the booking interface is clean, and availability is abundant. **What makes this easy:** - **No complex routing rules.** There's no geographic zone logic, no partner airline ticketing, no stopover rules to navigate. You pick a hotel, check availability, transfer points, and book. That's the entire process. - **Instant transfers.** Both Chase Ultimate Rewards and Bilt Rewards transfer to World of Hyatt instantly. You can go from zero Hyatt points to a confirmed reservation in under five minutes. - **Reliable availability.** Category 1 properties are upper-midscale hotels with large room inventories. Award availability is rarely the bottleneck at this tier. **The one thing to watch:** Points don't live in Hyatt until you transfer them — and they can't come back once transferred. Always search hyatt.com *first*, confirm your dates show award space, *then* transfer. This single habit eliminates the only real risk in the process. **Tips for first-timers:** 1. Create your free World of Hyatt account before you need it — having your membership number ready speeds the transfer process. 2. Start with a one-night stay to build confidence, then scale up. 3. Screenshot your confirmation email and points balance after booking — it feels good, and it's good record-keeping. If you've ever booked a hotel room online, you can execute this redemption. Go do it.

Category 1 primarily includes Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties in secondary markets, smaller cities, and suburban locations. These are upper-midscale hotels with consistently good quality — clean rooms, modern decor, and amenities like free Wi-Fi. Hyatt House properties often include complimentary breakfast and kitchen suites.

However, award availability itself can vary — popular properties during high-demand weekends may show no award availability even though the price remains 5,000 points when rooms are available.

At 5,000 points for a $100 to $200 room, you are getting 2 to 4 cents per point — two to four times the value of redeeming the same Chase Ultimate Rewards points as 1 cent per point cash back. Even compared to the Sapphire Reserve portal rate of 1.5 cents per point, Category 1 Hyatt bookings consistently deliver superior value. Note that Sapphire Preferred holders transfer at 4:3, so factor in the conversion when comparing.

Category 1 Hyatt hotels are the single best entry point into travel rewards for the FI community. At 5,000 points per night with cash values of $100 to $200, you consistently achieve 2 to 4 cents per point — a redemption rate that proves the system works before you ever attempt a complex international booking. This is the foundational redemption that builds your travel rewards confidence and conviction.

#8970. Former workshop converted into contemporary Japanese home with "a sense of the passage of time"

Japanese studio Akio Isshiki Architects has transformed the home and workshop of a sheet-metal craftsperson in the castle town of Tatsuno into a modern house with a latticed wooden gate.

Architect Akio Isshiki, the founder of the eponymous studio, said he had to take a lot of different aspects into consideration when designing the project.

Among them was the location, as the two-storey home is located in a historic town known for being built around a medieval mountain castle.

“The project explores an architecture that responds naturally to the many contexts and conditions surrounding the house: the historic streetscape of the former castle town, traces of the former owner’s work as a sheet-metal craftsman, the client’s wishes, and practical constraints such as building regulations and structural requirements,” Isshiki told Dezeen.

For example, while the client had initially wanted a deck that would be connected to the dining room, the compact site made such a design difficult.

Instead, Isshiki removed part of the existing interior of the dining room to create a terrace space, which also includes a traditional-style engawa platform to connect the home with the garden.

Here, the studio added a sliding glass door that was designed so that its frame is hidden in the wall when it is closed, creating the impression of a fully open space.

Isshiki also wanted the 144-square-metre contemporary home to nod to more traditional Japanese houses.

“To sit comfortably within the townscape that retains the character of a former castle town, the spatial principles of traditional machiya – Japanese old townhouses – have been incorporated into this contemporary residence,” he explained.

“Examples include a long approach leading towards a bright garden at the back of the house, and an engawa, a narrow platform that connects the interior with the garden.”

The former workshop in front of the house was treated as a public-facing space. Where it looks onto the street, Isshiki added a large latticed, sliding gate, made from cedar, as well as a narrow entrance porch.

Inside, this multi-functional space becomes almost like an enclosed terrace. Here, Isshiki also added a small wooden toilet, inspired by those found in traditional machiya houses.

The studio kept a number of objects that were found in the old workshop, including a metal ring that now decorates a handrail next to the indoor staircase.

Isshiki relocated this staircase so that it sits at the front of the house, in the old workshop space – one of the biggest changes made to the layout of the house. A stone underneath the first step provides a space to remove footwear.

Isshiki’s studio used wood throughout the renovation, as the original building was made from timber and this material worked best with the existing neighbourhood, including a historic shrine that stands directly across from the house.

“The newly added wood, including the doors, is cedar, which is also the primary wood used in the original structure,” Isshiki said.

“Cedar is one of the most widely used types of wood in Japan and is readily available,” he continued.

“The contrast between the lighter new cedar and the existing cedar, which has darkened with age, brings a sense of the passage of time to the house.”

Akio Isshiki Architects also used earthen plasterwork in the home to create a tactile feel, while Tunisian tiles add decorative patterns in the kitchen. Here, the studio also created a built-in, combined wooden dining table and work surface.

On the top floor, which has a bedroom, living room and guest room, the studio mostly kept the original layout.

However, it added a sunken study space and a tokonoma, a recessed area used to display flowers and pieces of art.

“Through careful consideration of spatial dimensions, light, connections to the outdoors, materials, details, and relationships between spaces, the aim was to create a home that feels comfortable as a whole,” Isshiki concluded about the renovation.

His studio has previously designed a charred-cedar-clad house in Osaka and married old and new within a combined home and restaurant.

#8969. demi nguyen balances corporate branding, fintech systems, and typographic archives

demi nguyen translates complex ideas into visual identities, digital experiences, and communication systems, balancing strategic precision with an expressive approach to storytelling.

Han On edited by christina vergopoulou November 6, 2026 3 min

Based in Dallas, Texas, designer Demi Nguyen develops brand identities, digital interfaces, editorial publications, and communication systems across the technology, media, and cultural sectors. Informed by lived experience across Vietnam, Hungary, and the United States, her practice pairs structured research with experimental typography and modular graphic systems tailored to technical corporate contexts and cultural archives alike.

Within corporate environments, Nguyen works as a graphic designer in the global creative operations division at Texas Instruments, producing campaign graphics, enterprise collateral, and commemorative event assets such as visual identities for Jack Kilby Day. Her independent projects examine the intersection of digital systems and user accessibility: Kivo, a speculative fintech identity developed as a capstone, translates financial services into an approachable visual system tailored to creative entrepreneurs via AI platform prototypes, landing pages, and marketing toolkits. Similarly, for consultancy Team Union, Nguyen devised a modular design framework spanning competitor benchmarks, pitch decks, Figma proposal templates, and custom spot illustrations.

Her cultural and public communication portfolio encompasses broadcast and digital graphics for North Texas public media outlet KERA, as well as institutional print collateral, campus illustrations, and a 166-page annual report for Texas Christian University. Nguyen’s self-initiated research explores media translation and vernacular typography: Creator investigates YouTube digital culture through printed publication layouts, while Vietype functions as an open digital archive cataloging Vietnamese hand-drawn lettering and signage produced between the 1960s and 1980s. A complementary documentary photography practice captures light, domestic interiors, and streetscapes, reinforcing an observational methodology rooted in legibility, context, and structural coherence.

#8968. Ultimate Guide to 4A Hair: Care Tips, Styles, and Maintenance

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

Alright, curl friends, let’s break it down. Hair type falls into four main categories:

Now, Type 4 hair is where things get seriously curly and coily. Within this category, we’ve got subtypes A, B, and C,

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Yes, 4A hair is curly and falls under the coily category. It features tight, springy curls that form an S-shape.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Love those natural curls — keep them hydrated, avoid excessive heat, and give them some nighttime TLC.

#8967. Holst completes Adjaye-designed mass-timber library in Oregon

Photography by Christian Columbres

US architecture studio Holst has created a mass-timber library in Oregon, with a series of tall columns at the entrance and a central atrium, after taking over the project from Adjaye Associates.

The East County Library in Gresham features a trapezoidal roof structure on top of a mostly square building envelope, creating multi-storey covered entry programmes on each side.

These entry programmes are lined with massive glued-laminated (glulam) mass-timber columns that Holst said speak to a primary effect of the design: “awe and accessibility”.

“One of our major main vision points of the project was this idea of awe and accessibility,” Holst principal and creative director Brittany Shreiner told Dezeen.

Shreiner said that the accessible component comes from the dual entry programmes that open up to a plaza on one side, with space taken from a converted street, and an elevated entryway on the other that features ramps.

A rail line is located on one side and a bus line on the other, connecting the building to the wider public realm.

For the team, the building needed to be a “big civic moment”, thus the massive columned entryway. However, Shreiner said that the awe the studio aspired to create was more akin to that of a forest, and the mass timber helped them to express that.

Structurally, the building has a mix of concrete and mass timber elements, with mostly wooden floorplates and some walls, and concrete-and-steel cores.

The facade is a mix of vertical timber elements interspaced with high-performance concrete bands with scalloped shapes and vertical bands of glass.

At one point, a grey-toned concrete panelling system marks the semi-circular protrusion where the structure’s amphitheatre is.

The appearance of the building is close to the original design submitted by Adjaye Associates – Holst was the architect of record at the start.

However, after misconduct allegations against Adjaye Associates founder David Adjaye were made public in a Financial Times investigation, the studio was released from this project, among others. Adjaye denies the allegations.

Shriener said that the biggest changes in the design were the removal of screens that were supposed to overhang from the covered entryways and a tower that extended past the roof plane.

“There was still a lot of design to be done [at that time], but the bones of the building were there. The community buy-in was there. The stakeholder buy-in was there,” said Shriener.

“So, the county was definitely clear in their intention that they did not want to proceed with Adjaye as part of our team, and that they basically trusted us to bring the project forward, but they didn’t want to see a total redesign by any means.”

Having recently solidified itself as a name in the US mass timber game with a tall building in Portland, the studio focused on optimising the timber usage as it took over the design. It worked closely with local mass-timber supplier TimberLab for the materials.

One detail that stands out is the notches in the timber columns and beams that give the structure a cabin-like or residential appearance, while remaining monumental in scale.

More than just a style conceit, the notches play a role in the ceiling plane, hiding the mechanical systems and lighting.

Inside, vestibules compress the entry to the library, which then opens up into a main core that runs between the entrances, with a double-height atrium space in the middle, complete with a wood-slatted spiral staircase.

For Shriener, this middle space represents a “clearing” in the forest.

The primary book-storage spaces surround the main central area, with smaller breakout rooms and classrooms lying mostly on the perimeter.

Mass-timber elements remain visible throughout the interior spaces, with green carpets at times continuing the forest metaphor.

On the roof, a series of sawtooth lightwells bring diffuse light into the main central space, while a rooftop patio allows guests to enjoy the views of the mountains beyond.

Elsewhere in Oregon, Holst created a Gaudí-informed apartment building wrapped in wood.

Other projects that were completed after the fallout from the Adjaye allegations include the Princeton Art Museum, where David Adjaye “stepped back” from the project in the late stages, according to Princeton.

Photography by Christian Columbres

#8966. Tatiana Bilbao creates rammed-earth installation at Art Omi

Mexico-based architecture practice Tatiana Bilbao Estudio has created a large-scale outdoor installation made of rammed earth derived from local soil that’s meant to break down over time for New York arts centre Art Omi.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio‘s Borrowed Earth installation consists of four 7.5-foot-tall rammed-earth cruciform crosses, with a shorter cross form in the centre that serves as a bench. Each form was made with compacted soil harvested from the Hudson Valley area.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio based the design around a “repeatable basic unit” that eventually became the bench and surrounding columns.

The Borrowed Earth piece was commissioned by arts centre Art Omi, which oversees a 120-acre sculpture park at its campus in Ghent, New York.

Art Omi curator Julia van den Hout said rammed earth can be a “challenging material”, and it shaped much of the project’s design.

“They were not always crosses in our initial conversations,” van den Hout told Dezeen.

“As we started getting into the reality of trying to figure out how to construct this – because rammed earth is a challenging material to work with – and thinking structurally about how this would be built up, during those conversations, [it] shifted to being a cruciform column.”

“It also really resonated [because] it has such a strong classic modernist shape.”

The Art Omi and Tatiana Bilbao Estudio teams constructed the columns on site with guidance from rammed-earth consultant Raíz Arquitectura studio based out of Mexico.

The team used soil from a construction site just down the road from Art Omi, according to van den Hout. They mixed it with sand and lime and then packed the mixture layer by layer into wooden formwork to create the sculptures.

Van den Hout says the installation is designed to decay over a period of about two years, although the team does not have “a strict answer” about how long it will last given external elements like weather.

“It’ll be an experiment,” she said. “We don’t quite know how fast it’s going to go. It is definitely soft. It crumbles. It’s lovely and tactile in that when you touch it, you really feel that sense that erosion can happen pretty easily. But simultaneously, they feel very stable.”

Recently, MOS Architects created a sculpture at Art Omi made of aluminium, while Young Projects installed a frayed, wooden pavilion at the park in 2024.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio completed a sprawling aquarium in 2023 in Mexico, where the studio is primarily based and also spoke to Dezeen in 2019 about the country’s rising generation of prominent female architects.

#8965. "Direct and unrefined" materials create tactile interior at Jeju restaurant by &Daughters

Canadian studio &Daughters used basalt, cork, concrete, thatch and wood to design Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver that features traditional touches in a contemporary interior.

The architect’s starting point for the design was the restaurant’s menu, which includes modern dishes developed by chef Dylan Kim, traditional dishes created by his mother, chef Myungseok “Julie” Suh and dishes that they created together.

“The restaurant exists in the space where these two narratives meet,” &Daughters principal Emma Sims told Dezeen.

“We began to think of tradition and reinterpretation as the foundation for the design, translating this relationship into a physical space through a specific set of people, places, materials and traditions.”

While Jeju’s exterior has a modern steel-mesh facade, the interior juxtaposes wood and concrete for a warmer, more tactile feel.

At the heart of the 44-seat restaurant is a reinterpretation of a traditional thatched house from Jeju Island, South Korea, called a chogajip.

This was constructed using lumber and hand-thatched grass, and creates an artisanal focal point for the space.

Other materials, including basalt, were chosen by &Daughters for Jeju to ensure a natural feel.

Basalt was used for the bar, chef’s table and host stand, while cork cladding helps create a soft feel while adding acoustic dampening.

The studio kept the existing concrete floor but polished it to reveal variations in its colour.

“The palette is quite simple – basalt, cork, raw concrete masonry units, polished concrete, wood and thatch,” Sims said.

“Basalt is one of the most recognisable materials of Jeju Island,” she continued.

“Formed through volcanic activity, it is found throughout the island’s landscape, architecture and traditional stone walls. Beyond that, we were interested in materials that felt direct and unrefined, allowing them to retain their natural character.”

The studio wanted to “introduce elements of tradition, ritual and memory into the interior,” Sims said.

As well as the thatched house, another traditional architectural feature from Jeju, a jeongnang three-pole gate, was also introduced to the interior.

“Historically used as a means of communicating whether a household was home, away or nearby, it offered an alternative to a conventional locked entrance, rooted in trust and shared understanding,” Sims said.

“At Jeju, we incorporated our interpretation into the glazing beside the entrance, where staff lower two poles each day to signal that the restaurant is open and guests are welcome, raising them again at the end of service,” she continued.

“In this way, a traditional architectural element becomes an active part of the restaurant’s daily life.”

Other restaurants recently featured on Dezeen include a brick-clad eatery in London’s Soho area and a bistro in Montreal influenced by Japanese metabolism.

#8964. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

#8963. lavazza tablì wins designboom special prize third place at seoul design award

lavazza's tablì tabs eliminates capsules from the single-cup experience.

Sustainability flourishes in simplicity. Caring for the planet becomes easy when real, convenient and functional alternatives replace more polluting options. Lavazza kept this reality in mind with Tablì, a capsule-free single-serve coffee system that has earned third place in the designboom Special Prize at the Seoul Design Award 2026.

Until now, coffee drinkers have had three main options: go through the hassle of preparing a pot each time they wanted to enjoy the drink, use instant coffee or turn to a capsule machine. The third option is widespread because of its convenience, but there is a hidden side that not everyone is aware of.

According to figures from Deutsche Umwelthilfe, cited by Lavazza in its award submission, around 20 billion coffee capsules are used, and therefore discarded, every year. Germany alone consumes around 3.4 billion, generating approximately 13,500 metric tons of waste annually.

Hailing from Italy, a country where coffee is both a rule and a tradition, the multidisciplinary team, led by Florian Seidl and joined by Angelica Rella, Marco Rotundo and Nicola Bettoni, was well aware of this problem.

The team posed a revolutionary question: what if there were another way to prepare coffee? Tablì was born from the ambition to replicate the convenience of capsule coffee while designing a product with minimal environmental impact.

Their vision went beyond replacing capsules with a less harmful form of packaging. Instead, they designed a system built around a tab made entirely of coffee. No plastic, aluminum, additives or coatings. Alongside the tabs, they completed the ecosystem by designing a compatible machine, packaging, accessories and a connectivity system.

Lavazza Tablì considers environmental care from production through maintenance and everyday use. The machine is made using post-consumer plastics, and its construction takes repairability and low energy consumption into account. Moreover, because the tabs are made entirely of coffee, they generate only organic waste.

This commitment to sustainability has been key to securing the Special Prize with designboom. The Seoul Design Award’s purpose is precisely to promote projects that have achieved harmony between people, society and the environment.

The designboom Special Prize introduces a series of additional requirements. Award-winning projects must connect with designboom’s values: Intentionally Curious, Disrupt Playfully, and Fearlessly Meaningful. Ultimately, they must demonstrate an ability to think outside the box, create products that bring us joy and pursue design that, beyond being beautiful, expresses a bold vision with functionality rooted in its very conception.

Lavazza Tablì has the honor of taking third place in the category for its attention to detail, aesthetics and functionality as a whole rather than as separate elements. The product’s specifications speak for themselves: the height-adjustable cup rest with a metal grid; the sliding opening for inserting the tab; and the transparent water tank that allows users to check the water level are examples of a project conceived for intuitive, smooth operation that elevates the user experience while protecting the environment.

#8962. SCAD alumni transform 18th-century staircase into colourful installation during Design Miami Paris

Savannah College of Art and Design (SCAD) has revealed a colourful tufted flooring installation at this year’s Design Miami.Paris, as seen in this exclusive video produced by Dezeen.

Los Angeles-based designer and SCAD alumnus Abel Macias covered the staircase in fabric as part of a wider showcase of alumni works on display at the historic L’hôtel de Maisons in Paris.

Macias transformed the 18th-century staircase using bright colours and shapes informed by the landscape of the American Southwest.

At the top of the staircase, SCAD fibres graduate and Associate Chair of Fine Arts Gretchen Wagner presented a colourful suspended sculptural installation made from accordion-folded paper cylinders.

The paper cylinders were embellished with embroidered beading and hung from the ceiling like a chandelier.

SCAD furniture design graduate Evan Baker presented a wood-grain credenza, while SCAD furniture design graduate Anne Weber Callahan showed two ceramic stools meant to mimic clay.

Meanwhile, SCAD fibres graduate Katie Hagen designed a natural-dyed silk organza weaving, which was displayed alongside six sculptural lamps made by SCAD industrial design graduate Marcelo Suro.

The lamps merge hand-blown glass and volcanic stone and were created this past year by Suro during SCAD’s Alumni Atelier residency in Lacoste, France.

Macias completed a BFA illustration in 2002 and Wagner undertook an MFA in painting in 2023 and a BFA in fibres in 2011. Baker finished a BFA in furniture design in 2025, while Callahan graduated with a BFA in furniture design in 2019. Hagen obtained her MFA in fibres in 2023 and an MA in production design in 2023.

Last year, SCAD debuted an intricate plaster-cast installation at its booth during Design Miami in Florida.

SCAD is the official university partner of Design Miami and will next exhibit at the fair’s flagship event in Miami Beach this December.

To learn more about SCAD, visit its website.

#8961. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

#8960. Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

By now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting users’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

Some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

On top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He says this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

On top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

“We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” says Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”

Sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

“During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu says. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu says. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

But GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, says Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.)

At the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu says losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

As mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

“Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she says. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying issues may benefit sexual health.

That means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

“Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he says. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.)

GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, says Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, says board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

Of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist users said the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

“Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he says. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”

For those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon says. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

In these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

“Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer says. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”

Desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer says. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec says, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

Working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

#8959. Alter design exhibition returns to Tokyo with AI-powered tea ceremony and washi paper furniture

The second edition of young designers’ exhibition Alter has opened in central Tokyo, featuring a glowing lung-like lamp and Japanese cedar stools made from every part of the log.

Alter is being held at Nihonbashi Mitsu Hall during the 10th iteration of Designart Tokyo, which is ongoing across the Japanese capital.

The show brings together work from 75 international creators, mostly in their 20s or 30s, united by a desire to “re-examine the value of product design” in an industry that the exhibitors say is growing increasingly rigid in its output.

Among the offerings on display is a group show of texture-heavy design pieces curated by Dutch designer Tim Teven.

Under the title At First Contact, it includes a bright green vessel by French designer Audrey Large. Complete with protruding, tentacle-like embellishments, the vase is typical of Large’s otherworldly style.

Nearby, Dutch creative Teun Zwets presents a wall-mounted, mirrored cabinet made of his recognisably glossy lacquered split wood, while Paris studio LS Gomma contributed a polyurethane rubber scone lamp with a glowing ribbed body that loosely resembles a pair of lungs.

“The pieces’ attention to surface resonates with traditions within Japanese craft, where the effects of making, material behaviour and use remain visible in the finished object,” said Teven, who selected pieces that draw attention to “reflection, gloss and wear”.

Elsewhere, Alter presents a “tea ceremony with no host” by Tariki Research Institute, created to invert traditional Japanese tea ceremonies.

Instead of a tea master choosing the right cup for the occasion, environmental data picked up by sensors at various locations around the world is translated into organic shapes by an AI algorithm and blow-moulded into unique vessels, from which visitors were encouraged to drink.

Bole is a project by London architecture studio Pan Projects, completed in collaboration with local forestry company Morisho and Nara-based wood specialist Morisuke Mei Tree Industry.

Working with the knowledge that a typical Japanese cedar tree yields five logs, each four metres long, the collaborators made eight stools from each of these logs, cut into simple discs to use every part of the log.

For Alter, the stools are presented as a large totemic column to highlight the process.

“Today in the mountains of Japan, the market value of logs is below the value of the labour of the people who grow and care for them,” explained the show organisers.

“Even though wood continues to flow through construction and manufacturing sites, most of its value never goes back to the forest. Bole was born as a response to this imbalance.”

Also on display is Capillary Drift, a project by Japanese designer Yuma Kano, washi paper specialist Gen Taniguchi of Nao Tesuki Washi, and artisan Kurara Omichi, who works at Uchida Dyeing Factory in Tokyo.

The trio is presenting a selection of stools, vessels and other material experiments made out of delicately dyed washi paper.

“Rather than seeing washi simply as a flat surface, we approach it as a complex network of interwoven fibres, seeking to reveal expressions hidden within the material itself,” said Taniguchi.

The inaugural Alter exhibition was shown during last year’s Designart Tokyo. At the time, the exhibition team spoke to Dezeen about their desire to revive the city’s “increasingly homogenous” design scene.

Designart Tokyo 2026 takes place from 30 October to 8 November 2026 at various locations across Tokyo, Japan. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#8958. What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

When I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a new wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

There’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz says.

It seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

Fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” says Fertz. “You are born young.”

It turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

Sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky says. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”

At school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

Research shows that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

“I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”

Even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

Italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

“Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”

Paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very important to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

At cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

In fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in New York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert says. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

The antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

In Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

“Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo says. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”

Indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

Italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

“The most important thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz says. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, plan outings, and get out of the house.”

According to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz says, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”

#8956. maison margiela celebrates tokyo flagship anniversary with toothpick-drawn manga

an abandoned electronics factory, strange signals, and a group of researchers set the scene for the factory at night, an illustrated story that explores transformation without erasing the past.

A former electronics factory, strange signals, and a group of researchers investigating an abandoned building set the scene for The Factory at Night, an original manga commissioned by Maison Margiela for the 20th anniversary of its Tokyo flagship in Ebisu. Created by Tokyo-based artist Takehito Moriizumi, the science-fiction story translates the history of the building into an illustrated narrative, with an unusual detail defining its visual identity: the manga is drawn using a toothpick. The limited-edition zine brings together illustration, architecture, fashion, and storytelling, extending the anniversary celebrations of the house.

The narrative begins when a group of electrical engineering researchers visits an abandoned electronics factory to investigate strange signals recently detected inside. As they move through the building, they encounter an environment that seems to hold traces of its former life. Machinery, exposed wiring, industrial structures, staircases, and fragments of everyday objects populate the pages. Their investigation eventually leads to a transformation that introduces something entirely new without completely erasing what existed before.

The visual language of the manga is built around detailed black-and-white illustrations. Architectural elements often dominate the compositions, with complicated structural frameworks, overlapping staircases, suspended platforms, and exposed technical infrastructure creating a dense environment around the characters. The factory feels almost like a character in its own right, its architecture providing both the atmosphere and the narrative framework for the researchers’ investigation.

Moriizumi moves between expansive architectural scenes and more intimate manga panels, introducing the people who inhabit this unusual environment. The illustrations bring fashion into the fictional world through mannequins, garments, and references to the history of the house. The decision to work with a toothpick adds an unexpected material dimension to the publication. At a time when digital illustration, generative imagery, and increasingly automated creative processes are becoming part of visual production, the choice of an unconventional drawing tool invites a closer look at the act of making.

The Maison Margiela Tokyo store occupies a former electrical control equipment manufacturing factory at 2-8-13 Ebisu Minami, a building the house took over in 2006. Its history began six years earlier, when Martin Margiela selected a 1940s traditional Japanese residence in the same neighborhood for the brand’s first-ever retail store. The original boutique opened in September 2000, in an unexpected location away from Tokyo’s established luxury shopping districts of Ginza and Omotesando. The choice reflected the designer’s longstanding relationship with Japan, a country he and the Antwerp Six had regularly visited throughout the 1980s and 1990s.

The house was transformed through one of the Maison’s most recognizable design gestures: Bianchetto, the practice of painting objects and surfaces white. Furniture, architectural elements, and even the property’s tree stumps were covered in white paint, while the original bathroom and shared spaces were retained. When the store had to relocate in 2006, Maison Margiela chose another unconventional building just a five-minute walk away. The former factory offered a different setting, but the approach remained consistent, with the house incorporating elements of its industrial history into the new retail environment rather than erasing its previous function.

The original industrial goods elevator became fitting rooms, a shipping container housed the men’s collection, and a corridor leading to the shoes was constructed entirely from used shoeboxes. Furniture, doors, and display cases salvaged from flea markets and shops across Europe were brought to Tokyo. Parts of the original residential boutique, including its old family bathroom, were also reconstructed inside the new location, creating a physical connection between the two buildings.

Published as part of MaisonMargiela/folders, the manga forms one part of a broader initiative documenting the house’s history, creative identity, and relationship with its surroundings. The first volume of The Factory at Night is released on November 5, 2026, as a limited-edition zine available at selected newsstands across Ebisu and at the Maison Margiela Tokyo store. A digital edition is also being made available internationally through Dropbox.

#8955. SOM unveils design for luxury waterfront development on Australian pier

International architecture studio SOM is set to transform a historic pier in Geelong, Victoria, into a waterfront destination culminating in a rounded high-rise.

SOM recently won the competition to design the 10,000-square-metre development for developers Gurner Group and Costa Property Group, which will add public space, apartments, a 200-room hotel, shops and restaurants over the water at Corio Bay.

The project will involve transforming and extending the existing Cunningham Pier, which was originally built in 1855 to give railway access to docking ships. It underwent major refurbishment in 1929, and now acts as a stretch of car parking spaces culminating in a restaurant and event space.

Envisioned as a pedestrianised waterfront destination, visitors will enter SOM’s revamped pier through a public square with water features.

A 34-storey building will rise at the end of the pier, which will surpass the 21-storey Miramar apartment tower to become Geelong’s tallest building.

Trefoil in plan, the tower’s form will resemble three combined cylinders that taper towards the top and bottom.

Lining the length of Cunningham Pier will be a series of buildings with rounded edges and layered terraces, designed by SOM to reference the movement of water and marine forms.

The luxury development will contain around 280 apartments and 12 waterfront villas with individual yacht berths.

Activity spaces and sports courts will be built on floating platforms.

SOM hopes the development will establish Cunningham Pier as “both a neighbourhood on the water and a destination for Geelong’s residents and visitors”.

“An elevated public promenade forms the organising spine of the proposal,” said SOM. “By positioning new construction alongside the historic pier, the design preserves the existing structure below while creating a pedestrian environment above.”

“Shops, restaurants, and places to gather would line the route, connecting the city to activities and views across Corio Bay.”

According to SOM, the redevelopment will involve creating new marine habitats at the pier to support biodiversity.

“This ecological ambition forms part of a broader approach that considers the waterfront as a place for both public life and marine life,” said the studio.

Other projects recently unveiled by SOM include a tiered skyscraper that rises on a waterfront site in Chicago, and plans to build a 20-storey data centre in Kansas City.
